1.html:
Why start here

The word "trading" conjures up screens full of charts, quick profits and videos of people in sports cars. The reality is far less glamorous: trading is a risk-management job, where you accept losing often in order to win a little more than you lose. Before learning a single technique, you need to know exactly what game you're playing, against whom, and by what rules. That's what this lesson is about.

Trading, investing, speculating: three different things

All three buy and sell financial assets. What sets them apart is the source of the expected gain and the time frame.

  • Investing means buying an asset for what it produces: a company's profits, dividends, a bond's interest. The investor holds for years. They win if the company creates value (exactly what you see in the finance course).
  • Trading means buying or selling to profit from a price movement, over a short to medium period (from a few seconds to a few weeks). The trader barely cares what the company is worth: they're trying to predict where the price will go, and above all to manage what happens if they're wrong.
  • Speculating, strictly speaking, means betting on a future change. All trading is speculation. The word becomes pejorative when you bet without a method and without a loss limit.

One sentence to remember it by: the investor buys a share of a business, the trader buys a price movement.

The point that changes everything: a negative-sum game

When you invest for the long term in the stock market, you benefit from growing wealth: companies make profits, the economy grows. Everyone can win at the same time. It's a positive-sum game.

Short-term trading is different. Over a single day, Airbus's real value barely changes. If you make €100 buying at €150 and selling at €152, someone else sold too early or bought too late. Before fees, it's a zero-sum game: some people's gains are other people's losses.

And there are fees: broker commissions, the spread (the gap between the buying price and the selling price, which we'll see in lesson 3), sometimes financing costs. Once fees are deducted, trading is a negative-sum game. To win, being as good as average isn't enough: you have to be clearly better than the other participants.

And who are those others? Banks, funds, high-frequency algorithms, professional traders with better data, lower costs and years of experience.

What the numbers say

In Europe, brokers offering CFDs (leveraged products widely used by retail traders) are required to display on their website the percentage of their retail clients who lose money. The figure is usually between 70% and 90%. Go and check for yourself on any CFD broker's website: the disclosure is mandatory.

This isn't meant to discourage you. It's to set the rules of the game from lesson 1: most people lose, and this course is first and foremost about understanding why, so that you're not one of those who lose for silly reasons.

The four main trading styles

They differ by the holding period of a position (the time between buying and selling).

StyleLength of a positionNumber of tradesWhat it demands
Scalpinga few seconds to a few minutesdozens a dayvery low fees, fast execution, total concentration
Day tradinga few minutes to a few hours, everything closed by the eveninga few a daybeing in front of the screen during market hours
Swing tradinga few days to a few weeksa few a monthan analysis in the evening, orders placed in advance
Position tradinga few weeks to a few monthsa few a yearpatience, accepting big swings along the way

The shorter the time frame, the more:

  • fees weigh heavily (you pay them on every round trip);
  • noise dominates (small random moves matter more than the real trend);
  • competition from machines is fierce.

That's why, for a student who can't spend all day in front of a screen, swing trading is generally the most realistic style. It's the one we'll favour in this course's examples.

The two main families of analysis

To decide when to buy and when to sell, traders rely on two approaches, often combined.

  • Technical analysis studies price and volume themselves, on charts. Its idea: everything known is already in the price, and human behaviour (fear, greed) leaves traces that repeat. This will be the bulk of modules 2 and 3.
  • Fundamental analysis studies what moves value: company results, interest rates, inflation, central bank decisions. That will be module 6, and your finance course is already preparing you for it.

Neither predicts the future. They help you spot situations where the odds are slightly in your favour.

What really makes a trader last

If you remember only one idea from this course, make it this one: you don't win by being right, you win by losing little when you're wrong.

A trader who wins 40% of their trades can be profitable if they gain €3 on average when they're right and lose €1 when they're wrong. A trader who wins 80% of their trades can be ruined if a single loss wipes out twenty wins. Module 4 (risk management) is therefore the most important in the course, even if it's the least spectacular.

The three pillars, which we'll come back to throughout the programme:

  1. A method: written rules for getting in and out, tested before putting money on them.
  2. Risk management: knowing before each trade how much you're willing to lose, and sticking to it.
  3. Psychology: applying the rules even when you're scared or desperate to win it back.

Key takeaways

  • Investing = benefiting from the value a company creates, over years. Trading = profiting from a price movement, over a short to medium period.
  • Short-term trading is a zero-sum game before fees, and negative-sum after fees: to win, you must be better than most other participants.
  • 70 to 90% of retail CFD accounts lose money (a mandatory disclosure for European brokers).
  • Four styles: scalping, day trading, swing trading, position trading. The shorter it is, the more fees and noise weigh.
  • For a student, swing trading is the most realistic style.
  • You win by losing little when you're wrong, not by always being right.

Exercise

  1. For each person, say whether they're more of an investor, a day trader, a swing trader or a scalper:
    1. Inès has bought TotalEnergies shares every month for 5 years to collect the dividends.
    2. Hugo buys Renault shares on Monday after a sharp fall and sells them 8 days later after a rebound.
    3. Malik places 200 orders a day on the DAX futures contract and holds each position for less than 2 minutes.
    4. Clara buys Bitcoin at 10:00, sells it at 15:00, and never has an open position in the evening.
  2. Hugo (the swing trader) makes 10 round trips a month. Each round trip costs him 0.3% of the amount committed in fees and spread. He commits €2,000 on each trade. How much do his fees cost him per month? And per year?
  3. Malik (the scalper) makes 200 round trips a day, at €2 in fees each, over 20 trading days a month. How much does he need to make per month just to cover his fees?
  4. Food for thought: a friend tells you he "wins 9 trades out of 10, so he must be profitable". What do you say to him?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Inès: investor (buying for dividends, holding for years). Hugo: swing trader (8 days). Malik: scalper (under 2 minutes, hundreds of trades). Clara: day trader (everything closed by the evening).
  2. Fees per trade: 2,000 × 0.3% = €6. Per month: 10 × 6 = €60. Per year: 60 × 12 = €720. If Hugo trades with €2,000 of capital, he has to make 36% a year just to break even. Fees are the trader's first opponent.
  3. 200 × €2 × 20 days = €8,000 a month in fees. Malik has to make €8,000 every month before he even starts making a profit. That's why scalping is only viable with extremely low fees, generally reserved for professionals.
  4. The win rate alone tells you nothing. If he makes €10 on each of his 9 good trades (€90) and loses €150 on the bad one, he's down €60 over 10 trades. What counts is the combination of win rate and the ratio between average gain and average loss. This is called expectancy, and we'll calculate it precisely in lesson 22.

Next lesson: the markets you can trade (shares, indices, forex, commodities, crypto) and their opening hours.

2.titre: The markets and their opening hours
2.html:
Why it matters

Last time, we saw that trading means profiting from a price movement. But the price of what? And when? You don't trade oil the way you trade an Airbus share, and you don't trade at 3 in the morning the way you do at 15:30. Each market has its own hours, its own players, its own way of moving. Choosing your market is often a trader's first decision, and it depends a lot on your timetable.

Shares: owning a piece of a company

A share (or stock) is a part of a company's capital. When you buy an LVMH share, you become (a very small) owner of LVMH. Its price rises and falls depending on what buyers and sellers think about the company's future: results, announcements, sector news.

Shares are traded on stock exchanges:

  • Euronext Paris for French shares (TotalEnergies, LVMH, Airbus...);
  • the NYSE and the Nasdaq in New York for US shares (Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia...);
  • the Deutsche Börse (Xetra) in Frankfurt, the London Stock Exchange, the Tokyo Stock Exchange, and so on.

What characterises shares: each stock has its own story. A share can jump 10% or drop 20% in one session on results day, even if the rest of the market doesn't move.

Indices: a market's weather report

An index is a basket of shares that summarises the state of a market. It's a thermometer.

IndexWhat it measures
CAC 40the 40 largest companies listed in Paris
DAX 40the 40 largest German companies
Euro Stoxx 50the 50 largest in the eurozone
S&P 500500 large US companies, the global benchmark
Nasdaq 100the 100 largest stocks on the Nasdaq, very tech-heavy

You can't "buy an index" directly: it's a calculation, not an object. To trade it, you go through a product that tracks it: an ETF (a listed fund that copies the index), a futures contract or a CFD. We'll go through these products in lesson 38.

Why traders like indices: they're very liquid (huge numbers of buyers and sellers), and an index can't go bust or lose 50% on one company's bad news. Its moves are "cleaner" than those of a single share.

Forex: the currency market

Forex (foreign exchange) is the market where you swap one currency for another. It's by far the largest financial market in the world: according to the Bank for International Settlements' 2022 survey, over 7.5 trillion dollars a day changed hands there.

You trade currency pairs. The most traded is EUR/USD:

EUR/USD = 1.0850 means that 1 euro is worth 1.0850 dollars.

If you think the euro will rise against the dollar, you buy EUR/USD. If you think it will fall, you sell it.

Currencies move little in percentage terms: a 1% move in EUR/USD in a day is already a big move. That's why forex is almost always traded with leverage, which makes it very dangerous for beginners (lesson 6). The unit of movement is called the pip: for EUR/USD, it's the 4th decimal place (0.0001).

What moves currencies: central bank interest rates (ECB, Fed), inflation, growth, politics. We'll come back to this in module 6.

Commodities

Gold, silver, oil (Brent for Europe, WTI for the US), gas, wheat, copper, coffee... They're traded mainly via futures contracts on exchanges such as the CME in Chicago, or via CFDs and ETFs.

  • Gold is a safe haven: it tends to rise when investors are scared or when real interest rates fall.
  • Oil reacts to geopolitics (Middle East, Russia), OPEC+ decisions and the health of the global economy. It can be very violent: in April 2020, in the middle of Covid, the May WTI contract even went below zero for a few hours, because nobody had any room left to store the oil being delivered.

Cryptocurrencies

Bitcoin, Ethereum and thousands of others. They're traded on platforms (Binance, Coinbase, Kraken...) rather than on a regulated exchange like Euronext.

Two particular features:

  1. They never close: 24/7, including Christmas Eve.
  2. They're extremely volatile: Bitcoin went from about $69,000 in November 2021 to about $15,500 in November 2022, a fall of more than 75% in a year. And it has seen equally spectacular rises.

Volatility means opportunities, but also fast losses. For a beginner, it's the trickiest market: it moves at night while you sleep, and many platforms push you to use huge leverage.

Opening hours: when each market is open

All times are given in Paris time (CET/CEST, one hour ahead of the UK).

MarketHours (Paris time)Note
Euronext Paris (French shares)9:00 – 17:30, Monday to Fridayclosing auction just after 17:30
Xetra (German shares)9:00 – 17:30same rhythm as Paris
NYSE / Nasdaq (US shares)15:30 – 22:00see the clock-change trap below
Forexfrom Sunday evening ~23:00 to Friday evening ~23:00, non-stopclosed at weekends
Futures contracts (indices, gold, oil)almost 24 hours a day on weekdaysshort break each day
Crypto24/7never closed

Forex sessions

Forex is open 24 hours a day, but it isn't equally active at every hour. It follows the sun around the globe:

  • Asian session (Tokyo, Sydney): night-time for us, fairly calm on EUR/USD.
  • European session (London): from about 9:00, much more active.
  • US session (New York): from about 14:00.

The busiest time of day is the London + New York overlap, roughly 14:00 to 18:00 (Paris time). That's when volumes are highest and when the big US statistics are released (often at 14:30).

The clock-change trap

Europe and the United States don't change their clocks on the same day. For one to three weeks in spring and autumn, the gap shrinks from 6 hours to 5, and Wall Street opens at 14:30 Paris time instead of 15:30.

A concrete example, coming up soon: in 2026, Europe switches to winter time on 25 October, the US on 1 November. Between those two dates, the New York stock exchange will therefore open at 14:30 Paris time. Lots of beginners get caught out every year.

Open, close and "gaps"

Markets are busier just after the open and just before the close: that's when the orders accumulated overnight are executed and big players adjust their positions.

When an exchange closes, news keeps coming in (results published in the evening, geopolitical events, the US session). The next morning, the price can therefore open noticeably higher or lower than the previous close, without going through the prices in between. This jump is called a gap.

Why it's dangerous: if you hold a position overnight with a protective order (stop) at €100, and the share opens at €92 the next day, your order will be executed around €92, not €100. The gap "jumped" over your stop. We'll see this again in lesson 4.

Which market for you?

There's no universal right answer, but there are a few simple criteria:

If you...Suitable markets
are in class all day and free in the eveningUS shares (15:30 – 22:00), with swing trading
want to understand what you're tradingshares and indices you know (CAC 40, French companies)
want "cleaner" movesindices rather than single shares
are just starting outavoid leveraged forex and crypto at first, the trickiest ones

For a student, a realistic combination: analyse in the evening, place your orders in advance, and trade shares or indices with swing trading. That's the basis we'll use in the examples in the coming lessons.

Key takeaways

  • Shares: a piece of a company; each stock has its own story and can move sharply on news.
  • Indices: a basket of shares (CAC 40, S&P 500...), traded via ETFs, futures or CFDs, more stable than a single share.
  • Forex: the largest market in the world; you trade pairs (EUR/USD), open 24 hours a day on weekdays, almost always with leverage.
  • Commodities: gold, oil..., mainly via futures contracts, sensitive to geopolitics.
  • Crypto: open 24/7, extremely volatile.
  • Paris: 9:00 – 17:30. New York: 15:30 – 22:00 (14:30 during the clock-change gap).
  • Opening gaps can jump over your protective order.
  • Choose your market according to your timetable and your level.

Exercise

  1. It's 16:00 in Paris on a Tuesday in January. Which of these markets are open? Euronext Paris, NYSE, forex, Bitcoin.
  2. It's 10:00 in Paris on a Saturday. Same question.
  3. EUR/USD goes from 1.0850 to 1.0920. Has the euro appreciated or depreciated against the dollar? By how many pips has it moved?
  4. You're in class from 8:00 to 18:00, then free from 19:00 to 23:00. Which stock market can you follow live? At what time (Paris time) will it open on 28 October 2026?
  5. A share closes on Friday at €50. You have a protective order to sell at €47. Over the weekend, the company announces a scandal, and the share opens on Monday at €41. At roughly what price is your sale executed, and how much do you lose per share compared with what you'd planned?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. All four are open: Euronext (9:00 – 17:30), the NYSE opened at 15:30, forex runs continuously on weekdays, and Bitcoin never closes. It's actually the most active slot of the day (the Europe / US overlap).
  2. Only Bitcoin (and other crypto). Stock exchanges and forex are closed at weekends.
  3. The price of the euro in dollars has risen, so the euro has appreciated against the dollar. Change: 1.0920 − 1.0850 = 0.0070, i.e. 70 pips (1 pip = 0.0001). As a percentage: 0.0070 / 1.0850 ≈ 0.65%, which is already a notable move for a currency.
  4. US shares (NYSE, Nasdaq), open until 22:00 Paris time. On 28 October 2026, Europe is already on winter time (since the 25th) but the US isn't (1 November): Wall Street will therefore open at 14:30 Paris time. For you, it changes nothing, since you only get there at 19:00.
  5. The market opens straight at €41, never passing through €47: your order is triggered and executed around €41 (or a bit lower). You expected to lose at most €3 per share (50 − 47); in reality you lose about €9 (50 − 41), three times more than planned. That's gap risk, and one more reason never to commit too much to a single position.

Next lesson: how a price is formed. The order book, the bid, the ask, the spread and liquidity.

3.html:
Why it matters

On your app, you see "Airbus: €150.00". That figure looks simple, almost official. In reality, there's no single "Airbus price": at every moment there are people ready to buy a little cheaper, and people ready to sell a little dearer. The price is simply the last place where a buyer and a seller agreed. Understanding this mechanism will stop you paying hidden costs without realising, and will explain why your order doesn't always fill at the price you saw.

The order book: the queue of buyers and sellers

On an exchange such as Euronext, all pending orders are lined up in an order book. On one side, the buyers with the maximum price they're willing to pay. On the other, the sellers with the minimum price they're willing to accept.

Here's a simplified, fictional order book for a share:

Buyers: quantityBuyers: priceSellers: priceSellers: quantity
300€149.95€150.00200
500€149.90€150.05400
800€149.85€150.10600
1,200€149.80€150.15900

How to read it:

  • The best buying offer is at €149.95: someone wants to buy 300 shares at that price, no higher. That's the bid.
  • The best selling offer is at €150.00: someone wants to sell 200 shares at that price, no lower. That's the ask (or offer).
  • As long as nobody gives way, nothing happens: buyers wait below, sellers above.

A trade happens when someone accepts the other side's price. If an impatient buyer agrees to pay €150.00, they buy from the cheapest seller. The displayed "price" then becomes €150.00.

Bid, ask and spread

Bid = the best price at which you can sell right now (the price buyers are offering).

Ask = the best price at which you can buy right now (the price sellers are asking).

Spread = Ask − Bid.

In our example: spread = 150.00 − 149.95 = €0.05, or about 0.03% of the price.

Why is that a cost? Imagine you immediately buy 100 shares at the ask (€150.00), then change your mind and sell straight back at the bid (€149.95). The price hasn't moved, and yet you've lost 100 × 0.05 = €5, not counting brokerage fees. The spread is the price of impatience: whoever wants to be filled right away pays it to whoever is willing to wait.

That's why we say a position always starts slightly in the red: you buy at the ask, but your position is valued at the price you could sell it for, the bid.

The spread at CFD and forex brokers

Many brokers advertise "€0 commission". They then earn part of their money on the spread, which they widen a little. The spread becomes your hidden commission. Before choosing a broker (lesson 5), always compare the real spreads, not just the advertised fees.

Liquidity: the depth of the market

A market is liquid when there are lots of buyers and sellers, with big quantities, at very close prices. In practice, that means:

  • a tight (small) spread;
  • a deep order book (lots of quantity at each price level);
  • the ability to buy or sell large quantities without moving the price.
ExampleLiquidityTypical spread
EUR/USD in the middle of the dayenormousvery small
Large CAC 40 share (TotalEnergies, LVMH)highoften a single tick
Small, thinly traded companylowcan exceed 1% of the price
Small obscure cryptocurrencyvery lowcan be huge, and variable

Liquidity changes during the day: it's lower right at the open, late in the evening, during holidays and overnight for forex. The spread then widens. During a major announcement (a Fed decision, company results), sellers and buyers often pull their orders from the book out of caution: the spread can widen sharply for a few seconds or minutes.

When your order "walks" the book: slippage

Go back to our order book. You want to buy 800 shares right now, at market. There are only 200 shares at €150.00. Your order will therefore "eat through" several levels:

LevelQuantity takenPriceCost
1200€150.00€30,000
2400€150.05€60,020
3200€150.10€30,020
Total800€120,040

Your average price is 120,040 / 800 = €150.05, not €150.00 as displayed. This gap between the price you saw and the price you get is called slippage.

On a large, very liquid share, with a student's amounts, slippage is almost always negligible. It becomes significant:

  • on small, thinly traded stocks;
  • during announcements and moments of panic;
  • when your protective order triggers in a fast-falling market (we saw this with gaps in lesson 2).

Who's in the order book?

  • Market makers: specialist firms that constantly place buy and sell orders on both sides of the book. They earn the spread thousands of times a day, and in return they provide liquidity.
  • Institutions: funds, banks, insurers. They buy or sell very large quantities, often chopped into small pieces by algorithms so as not to move the price.
  • High-frequency traders: algorithms that react in microseconds.
  • Retail traders: you. A drop in the ocean, which has one advantage: your orders don't move the market.

Why the price really moves

The price rises when buyers are in more of a hurry than sellers: they accept the asking prices and "eat" the sell orders, level after level. The price falls when it's the sellers who are in a hurry and accept the prices offered by buyers.

Good news (better-than-expected results, for example) doesn't make the price rise by magic: it makes lots of people want to buy right now, while sellers raise their prices. It's this imbalance between impatient buyers and impatient sellers that charts record, and that you'll learn to read in module 2.

Key takeaways

  • The displayed price is the last traded price, not a single fixed price.
  • The order book lines up buyers (below) and sellers (above).
  • Bid = the price at which you can sell right now. Ask = the price at which you can buy right now. Spread = ask − bid.
  • The spread is a cost you pay on every round trip: a position always starts slightly in the red.
  • A liquid market has a tight spread and a deep book. Liquidity drops at the open, at night and during announcements.
  • A large market order can "walk" through several levels: that's slippage.
  • The price rises when buyers are more impatient than sellers, and vice versa.

Exercise

  1. A share shows: bid €42.10, ask €42.14. What's the spread in euros and as a percentage of the price (use the ask as the base)?
  2. You buy 250 shares at market, then immediately sell them at market. How much do you lose because of the spread alone?
  3. Using the order book from the lesson, you want to sell 1,000 shares immediately at market. Calculate your average selling price and the slippage compared with the displayed bid (€149.95).
  4. Two shares cost about €20. Share A has a spread of €0.01, share B a spread of €0.30. You plan to make 30 round trips a year of €2,000 on one of them. How much does the spread cost you over a year for each?
  5. Food for thought: the Fed publishes an important decision at 20:00 Paris time. Why is it a bad idea to place a market order on EUR/USD at 19:59?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Spread = 42.14 − 42.10 = €0.04. As a percentage: 0.04 / 42.14 ≈ 0.095%, roughly 0.1%.
  2. You buy at €42.14 and sell at €42.10: 250 × 0.04 = €10 lost, purely because of the spread (before brokerage fees).
  3. You sell by "eating" the buyers from the top down: 300 at €149.95 = €44,985; 500 at €149.90 = €74,950; the remaining 200 at €149.85 = €29,970. Total: €149,905 for 1,000 shares, an average price of €149.905. Slippage: 149.95 − 149.905 = €0.045 per share, or €45 in total compared with the displayed price.
  4. With €2,000 at €20, you trade 100 shares. Spread cost per round trip: A = 100 × 0.01 = €1; B = 100 × 0.30 = €30. Over 30 round trips: A = €30, B = €900 a year. Same strategy, same capital, and an €870 difference just because of liquidity. Illiquid shares are very expensive to trade often.
  5. Just before a big announcement, market makers pull some of their orders: the spread widens and the book gets thin. Your market order may fill at a much worse price than expected. And a second after the announcement, the price can jump in any direction. A simple rule when starting out: no market orders just before or just after a major announcement.

Next lesson: order types. Market orders, limit orders, stops and stop-limits, and which to use in which situation.

4.html:
Why it matters

Last time, we saw that the price comes from buyers and sellers meeting in the order book. Today we cross to the other side: how you get into that book. Because "buy 50 Airbus shares" means nothing until you've specified at what price and on what condition. The order type you choose decides whether you're filled right away or not at all, at what price, and above all how much you'll lose if the market goes against you. It's the first concrete tool of risk management.

The market order: "right now, at any price"

A market order simply says: "buy (or sell) immediately, at the best available price". Remember lesson 3: a market buy takes the ask, a market sell takes the bid.

  • Advantage: execution is almost certain and immediate (as long as the market is open and liquid).
  • Drawback: you don't control the price. You pay the spread, and if your order is large or the book is thin, you suffer slippage.

Market order = priority to execution, not to price.

It's reasonable on a large liquid share, mid-session, for a small quantity. It's dangerous at the open, just before an announcement, or on a small, thinly traded stock.

The limit order: "at this price or better, or nothing"

A limit order sets a maximum price when buying, or a minimum price when selling.

  • A buy limit at €148 will execute at €148 or less, never higher.
  • A sell limit at €160 will execute at €160 or more, never lower.

If the price never reaches your limit, the order stays in the book and doesn't execute. In fact your order becomes a line in the order book from lesson 3: you're one of those waiting, and you're the one who earns the spread instead of paying it.

Limit order = priority to price, not to execution.

Example (fictional): Airbus trades at €150. You think a dip towards €148 would be a better opportunity. You place a buy limit for 50 shares at €148. If the share drops to €148, you're filled. If it heads straight back up to €155, you've missed the move, but you haven't lost anything.

A limit order is also used to take profits: you buy at €150 and immediately place a sell limit at €160. If the price gets there, you exit without needing to be at your screen. This is what many platforms call a take profit.

The stop order: your seatbelt

A stop order (or "trigger order") sleeps until the price touches a given level, then wakes up and becomes a market order.

The sell stop (stop loss)

This is the single most important use in this whole course. You buy 50 shares at €150 and decide that if the share falls to €142, your idea was wrong. You place a sell stop at €142. If the price touches €142, the order turns into a market sell and your position is closed.

Planned loss = quantity × (entry price − stop price)

Here: 50 × (150 − 142) = €400 (before fees).

You know your maximum loss before getting in. That's exactly what you'll need in module 4 to calculate your position sizes.

The buy stop

Stops work for buying too, above the current price. Example: a share has been stuck at €55 for weeks and trades at €53. You only want to buy if it breaks through €55. You place a buy stop at €55.20: as long as the price stays below, nothing happens; if it goes through €55.20, you buy at market. It's the tool of the breakout strategy (lesson 26).

The limitation of a stop: it doesn't guarantee the price

A stop becomes a market order, so it executes at the next available price. Remember the gap from lesson 2: if the share closes at €145 in the evening and opens at €138 the next morning after bad news, your stop at €142 executes around €138. Your loss becomes 50 × (150 − 138) = €600 instead of €400. A stop limits the damage, it doesn't eliminate it.

The stop-limit order: a stop that refuses to sell cheap

A stop-limit order has two prices: a trigger and a limit. When the trigger is touched, it becomes a limit order (not a market order).

Example: sell stop-limit, trigger €142, limit €141. If the price drifts down calmly to €142, the order triggers and sells between €142 and €141. But if the share opens straight at €138, the order triggers, becomes "sell at €141 minimum"... and nobody buys at €141. You're left holding your shares, which may keep falling.

OrderTriggersBecomesExecution guaranteed?Price guaranteed?
Marketimmediately-yes (almost)no
Limitimmediately-noyes (your limit or better)
Stopwhen the trigger is touchedmarket orderyes (almost)no
Stop-limitwhen the trigger is touchedlimit ordernoyes (your limit or better)

To protect a position, most traders prefer a plain stop: better to get out at a bad price than not get out at all. The stop-limit is more useful on entry, for example to buy a breakout without paying any old price if the market runs away.

Practical options: duration and combined orders

How long does your order live?

  • Day: the order is cancelled at the close if it hasn't executed.
  • Until date: valid until a date you choose.
  • Good till cancelled (GTC): valid until you cancel it (often with a maximum duration set by the broker, check yours).

Classic trap: a "good till cancelled" order forgotten for three weeks that executes on a day when you no longer want it. Keep your pending orders tidy.

Combined orders

  • OCO (one cancels the other): two linked orders; when one executes, the other is cancelled. Typically a take profit at €160 and a stop at €142 on the same position.
  • Trailing stop: a stop that automatically moves up when the price rises, at a fixed distance (in euros or %), but never moves back down. It lets you protect a gain without capping the upside.

Trailing stop example (fictional): you buy at €50 with a 5% trailing stop. The stop starts at €47.50. The share climbs to €60: the stop follows and ends up at 60 × 0.95 = €57. Then the share falls back: the stop stays at €57 and takes you out around €57. You've made about €7 per share, without having to decide when to sell.

Not every broker offers all these orders on every market. Before trading, check which ones are available with yours (we'll talk about this in lesson 5).

Which order for which situation?

SituationSuitable order
Buy a dip towards a specific pricebuy limit
Buy only if the price breaks through a levelbuy stop (or stop-limit)
Cut a loss if the idea is wrongsell stop
Bank a gain at a targetsell limit (take profit)
Let a gain run while protecting ittrailing stop
Get out immediately, whatever happenssell at market

A rule to engrave right now: every position has its stop, placed at the moment of entry. Not "later", not "if it really falls". It's one of the major differences between the rare traders who last and the majority who lose.

Key takeaways

  • Market order: immediate execution, uncontrolled price (spread, slippage).
  • Limit order: controlled price (your limit or better), but execution not guaranteed.
  • Stop order: triggers at a threshold and becomes a market order. It's the stop loss tool.
  • A stop doesn't guarantee the price: a gap can make it execute much lower.
  • Stop-limit: becomes a limit order, and risks not executing at all.
  • Planned loss = quantity × (entry − stop), to be known before getting in.
  • Every position has its stop, placed on entry.

Exercise

  1. Which order type would you use in each case?
    1. You want to buy Danone only if it drops back to €58.
    2. You want to sell your position immediately, before the close.
    3. You want to buy a share that's stuck at €32 only if it goes above that level.
    4. You want to be taken out automatically if your position loses too much.
  2. You buy 40 shares at €75 with a sell stop at €71. What's your planned loss (before fees)? The next day, the share gaps down and opens at €68. What's your approximate actual loss?
  3. Same situation, but with a stop-limit: trigger €71, limit €70.50. The share opens at €68 and doesn't recover. What happens?
  4. You buy 100 shares at €50 with a 5% trailing stop. The share rises to €60, then falls back to €52. At what price (roughly) do you exit, and what's your total gain?
  5. Food for thought: why is it so important to place your stop at the moment you enter a position, and not later?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. a) Buy limit at €58. b) Sell at market (checking the spread). c) Buy stop a little above €32 (for example €32.10), possibly a stop-limit so as not to overpay. d) Sell stop (stop loss).
  2. Planned loss: 40 × (75 − 71) = €160. With the gap, the stop triggers and executes around €68: 40 × (75 − 68) = €280, i.e. 75% more than planned.
  3. The €71 trigger is crossed and the order becomes "sell at €70.50 minimum". But the market is at €68: nobody buys at €70.50. The order doesn't execute, you keep your 40 shares and your unrealised loss is already €280, with no protection left. That's why a plain stop is preferred for exits.
  4. The stop starts at €47.50, then follows the rise. At the high (€60), it's at 60 × 0.95 = €57. When the share falls back, the stop stays at €57 and triggers: you exit around €57 (not €52). Gain: 100 × (57 − 50) = about €700, before fees.
  5. Before getting in, you're clear-headed: you have no money at stake yet, so you can calmly decide where your idea becomes wrong. Once you're losing, emotions take over: you hope, you wait "for it to come back", you move the stop. Placing the stop on entry means making the hard decision when you're at your most rational. And it's essential for calculating your position size (lesson 21).

Next lesson: choosing your broker, understanding fees, and how trading is taxed in France (CTO, PEA, flat tax).

5.html:
Why it matters

We saw it in lesson 1: trading is a negative-sum game because of fees. The broker you choose, how it makes its money and the tax wrapper you use can make the difference between a slightly winning strategy and a losing one. These topics are less exciting than charts, but every euro saved here is a euro earned for certain, without taking any market risk.

The broker: your gateway to the market

You can't send an order to Euronext yourself: you have to go through an authorised intermediary, the broker. It passes on your orders, holds your securities and your money, and provides the platform. Broadly, there are four families:

TypeStrengthsWeaknesses
Traditional banksimple if you already bank there, PEA often availablegenerally high fees, limited platform
Online brokerlower fees, more complete tools, PEA and CTOpricing needs close comparison
Neo-broker (mobile app)very low or even "free" fees, very simplesometimes limited order types and markets, less visible revenue model
CFD / forex brokerleverage, short selling, access to every marketyou often trade against it (see below), and 70 to 90% of clients lose

Safety checks

  • The broker must be authorised: in France, you can check the public register of financial agents (REGAFI) and the blacklists of the AMF (the French financial markets regulator), which regularly publishes unauthorised websites. (In the UK, the equivalent is the FCA register.)
  • Be wary of any "broker" who contacts you by phone or messaging app, promises returns, or pushes you to deposit more. We'll come back to these scams in lesson 37.

How your broker makes money (and you lose it)

Here are the main fees to look for in the price list (a mandatory document, often called "pricing" or "fee schedule"):

  • Brokerage commission: the fee per order. It can be fixed (for example €2 per order), proportional (for example 0.1% of the amount) or a mix (a percentage with a minimum).
  • The spread: especially at CFD brokers and in forex, this is often their main source of income (lesson 3).
  • Currency conversion fees: if you buy a US share with euros, the broker converts your euros into dollars, then your dollars back into euros when you sell. It takes a margin on each conversion, often around 0.1% to 0.5% (check yours).
  • Financing costs: when you use leverage or hold a CFD overnight (lesson 6).
  • Other fees: custody fees, inactivity fees, real-time market data fees, withdrawal fees.

The real cost of a round trip = commission on buying + commission on selling + spread + any currency conversion fees.

The special case of the "market maker" broker

Many CFD brokers are themselves the counterparty to your orders: when you buy, they're the ones selling. It isn't illegal (it's regulated), but it means your losses can be their gains. Bear that in mind when a platform offers you bonuses, endless notifications or nudges you to trade more.

Example: comparing two (fictional) brokers

Broker A charges 0.5% with a €5 minimum. Broker B charges a fixed €2 per order. You place orders of €2,000, and make 40 round trips a year (so 80 orders).

Broker ABroker B
Fees per €2,000 order2,000 × 0.5% = €10€2
Fees per round trip€20€4
Fees per year (40 round trips)€800€160

Same strategy, and a €640 difference a year. If your capital is €5,000, broker A costs you 16% of your capital every year, broker B just over 3%. For an active trader, choosing a broker is a strategic decision.

The wrappers: CTO and PEA

In France, to trade shares directly, you open a securities account in one of these two wrappers. They don't change the markets; they change what you're allowed to do and how you're taxed.

The ordinary securities account (CTO, compte-titres ordinaire)

  • Anything goes: shares from all over the world, ETFs, bonds, derivatives depending on the broker.
  • No cap on deposits.
  • Capital gains are taxed every year (see the flat tax below).

The equity savings plan (PEA, plan d'épargne en actions)

  • Limited to European shares (European Union and European Economic Area) and eligible funds or ETFs.
  • Only one PEA per person, with a deposit cap (€150,000 for the standard PEA at the time of writing, to be checked).
  • No leverage, no short selling, no CFDs, no direct US shares.
  • Very favourable tax treatment after 5 years: gains are no longer subject to income tax, only to social charges. A withdrawal before 5 years normally means the plan is closed and the gains taxed (with a few exceptions).

The PEA is mainly aimed at long-term investing (finance course) — roughly the French counterpart of a UK stocks and shares ISA. For swing trading European shares it can be used, but with fewer tools.

Tax: the flat tax

In France, gains made on a CTO (capital gains on shares, gains on CFDs and other products) normally fall under the single flat-rate levy (PFU, prélèvement forfaitaire unique), nicknamed the flat tax. It's made up of income tax (12.8%) plus social charges.

Flat tax = 12.8% income tax + social charges, i.e. 30% for many years, then about 31.4% for most investment income from 2026. These rates change: always check the rate currently in force.

In this course's examples, we'll use 30% to keep the calculations simple. Key points:

  • You're taxed on the net capital gain for the year: gains minus losses realised during the year.
  • Unused capital losses can be carried forward against gains in the following years (for 10 years, under current rules).
  • Only realised gains count: as long as you haven't sold, there's no tax.
  • You can opt, across all your income of this type, for the progressive income tax scale instead of the 12.8%: this can be worthwhile if your marginal rate is low (often the case for students). Look into it when doing your tax return.

Worked example (fictional)

Over the year, on your CTO, you've realised €2,500 of capital gains and €1,000 of capital losses.

  • Net capital gain: 2,500 − 1,000 = €1,500.
  • Flat tax at 30%: 1,500 × 30% = €450.
  • Net gain after tax: €1,050.

The same €1,500 gain in a PEA held for over 5 years would only bear social charges: at the historical rate of 17.2%, about €258 (this rate has changed too, to be checked).

A few administrative traps

  • A French broker sends you an IFU (imprimé fiscal unique, an annual tax summary) every year listing your gains: the amounts are often pre-filled in your tax return.
  • With a foreign broker, it's up to you to calculate and declare everything, and you must normally declare the existence of the foreign account (form 3916). Forgetting can cost you a fine.
  • The financial transaction tax (TTF) applies to purchases of shares in large French companies (market capitalisation over one billion euros), at a rate of around 0.3% to 0.4% depending on the year. A purchase sold again the same day is generally not subject to it. Your broker deducts it automatically.
  • Cryptocurrencies have their own regime, different from that of shares.

This course isn't tax advice: for your own situation, refer to impots.gouv.fr (the French tax authority's website) or a professional.

Key takeaways

  • Choose an authorised broker and check it (REGAFI, AMF blacklists).
  • The cost of a round trip = commission × 2 + spread + any currency conversion. Compare price lists based on your order size.
  • For an active trader, a few euros per order adds up to hundreds of euros a year.
  • CTO: anything goes, gains taxed every year. PEA: European shares only, no leverage, favourable tax after 5 years.
  • Flat tax: 12.8% + social charges, about 30% (31.4% from 2026 for most income), on the year's net capital gain.
  • Tax rules change: always check the rates in force.

Exercise

  1. Broker A charges 0.1% with a €2 minimum. Broker B charges a fixed €5. How much does a €1,500 order cost with each? And an €8,000 order? From what order size does B become cheaper than A?
  2. You make 50 round trips of €1,500 a year. How much do commissions cost you per year with A and with B?
  3. You buy €2,000 of a US share, with currency conversion fees of 0.25% on each conversion. How much does conversion cost you over a round trip (assuming the price doesn't move)?
  4. On your CTO this year: €3,200 of capital gains, €1,400 of capital losses. Calculate the tax with a 30% flat tax, then your net gain after tax.
  5. Food for thought: your friend wants to swing trade US shares and sometimes sell short. He's hesitating between a PEA and a CTO. What do you explain to him?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. €1,500 order: A = 1,500 × 0.1% = €1.50, but the minimum applies, so €2; B = €5. €8,000 order: A = 8,000 × 0.1% = €8; B = €5. They cost the same when 0.1% of the amount equals €5, i.e. 5 / 0.001 = €5,000. Above that, B is cheaper; below it, A is cheaper.
  2. 50 round trips = 100 orders. A: 100 × €2 = €200. B: 100 × €5 = €500. With small orders, the proportional broker with a small minimum wins.
  3. On buying: 2,000 × 0.25% = €5. On selling: also about €5. Total ≈ €10 per round trip, i.e. 0.5% of the amount, on top of commission and spread. Over 40 round trips, that's already €400.
  4. Net capital gain: 3,200 − 1,400 = €1,800. Tax: 1,800 × 30% = €540. Net gain: 1,800 − 540 = €1,260. (At a 31.4% rate, the tax would be €565.20.)
  5. The PEA is ruled out for his project: it accepts neither direct US shares nor short selling. He needs a CTO, whose gains will be taxed every year at the flat tax. He should also keep an eye on currency conversion fees and, if he uses a foreign broker, his reporting obligations. He can still open a PEA alongside it for his long-term investing.

Next lesson: buying, short selling, leverage and margin, or how to win (and above all lose) faster.

6.html:
Why it matters

So far, we've imagined a trader who buys a share and hopes to sell it for more. But traders can also make money when the price falls, and commit more money than they have. These two tools, short selling and leverage, are pushed by every platform. They're also the two main reasons why so many retail accounts melt away in a few weeks. This lesson wraps up module 1: you need to understand them perfectly before you touch them.

Buying: the long position

Buying an asset in the hope that it rises means taking a long position (you're "long"). That's what you do when you buy 50 shares at €150.

  • Your gain if the price rises is theoretically unlimited (a share can double, triple...).
  • Your loss is limited to your stake: at worst, the share falls to 0 and you lose your €7,500, no more.

Short selling: the short position

Short selling means selling an asset you don't own, betting that it will fall, so you can buy it back later for less. You're "short", or you're "shorting".

How is that possible?

Your broker borrows the shares for you (from other clients or institutions that hold them). You sell them immediately at the market price. Later, you buy them back and return them to the lender. With CFDs (lesson 38), the mechanism is simplified: you just open a "sell" position.

Gain (or loss) on a short = quantity × (selling price − buy-back price)

Example (fictional): a share trades at €60. You short 100 shares.

  • It falls to €54 and you buy back: 100 × (60 − 54) = +€600.
  • It rises to €70 and you buy back: 100 × (60 − 70) = −€1,000.

The dangerous asymmetry

Shorting flips the risk profile of buying:

Long positionShort position
You win if...the price risesthe price falls
Maximum gainunlimitedlimited (the price can't go below 0)
Maximum lossyour stake (the price goes to 0)theoretically unlimited (the price can rise without end)

When lots of short sellers get caught out by a rise, they all have to buy back at the same time to limit their losses, which pushes the price up even further: that's a short squeeze. The famous example is GameStop in January 2021, whose share price rose more than tenfold in a few weeks.

The costs of shorting

  • Borrowing fees on the shares, which can be high on heavily "shorted" stocks.
  • If the share pays a dividend while you're short, you're the one who pays it to the lender.
  • In France, the PEA doesn't allow shorting; on a CTO, you go through CFDs, derivatives, or the deferred settlement service (SRD, service de règlement différé) that some brokers offer on large stocks, for a fee.

A short isn't "immoral" or reserved for pros: it's simply a bet on a fall. But it demands an even more disciplined stop than a purchase.

Leverage: playing with more than you have

Leverage lets you take a position larger than your capital. With leverage of 10, €1,000 lets you control a €10,000 position.

Exposure = margin × leverage

Change in your account (%) ≈ change in price (%) × leverage

Leverage doesn't change the market's direction; it multiplies everything: gains and losses alike. And fees, calculated on the exposure, are multiplied too.

Worked example (fictional)

You have €1,000 in your account. You buy a CFD on the CAC 40 for an exposure of €10,000, with leverage of 20.

  • Margin locked up: 10,000 / 20 = €500.
  • The CAC rises 2%: gain = 10,000 × 2% = +€200, i.e. +20% on your account.
  • The CAC falls 2%: loss = −€200, i.e. −20% on your account.

A 2% move in an index happens regularly, sometimes in a single session. With this leverage, one bad day wipes out a fifth of your capital.

Margin, margin calls and liquidation

Margin is the amount the broker locks up as collateral to let you open the position. If your losses eat into your account, it won't wait until you're at zero.

  • The margin call: the broker warns you that your account is nearing the minimum. You must add money or reduce your position.
  • Liquidation (stop out): if the account falls below a threshold, the broker closes your positions automatically, at the worst moment, without asking you.

For CFDs sold to retail clients in the European Union, the rule (set by ESMA in 2018 and adopted by the AMF; the UK's FCA has equivalent rules) requires positions to be closed when the account value falls to 50% of the required margin.

Back to the example: required margin €500. Liquidation happens when your account is worth 50% × 500 = €250, that is after a loss of 1,000 − 250 = €750. On a €10,000 exposure, all it takes is a fall of 750 / 10,000 = 7.5% in the CAC 40 to lose three quarters of your capital and get kicked out.

Maximum leverage for retail clients (CFDs, European Union)

UnderlyingMax leverageMinimum margin
Major currency pairs (EUR/USD...)303.33%
Major indices, gold, other currencies205%
Other commodities and minor indices1010%
Individual shares520%
Cryptocurrencies250%

These rules also require negative balance protection: a retail client can't lose more than the money deposited in their CFD account. Be careful: platforms outside the European Union offer leverage of 100, 500 or more, without these protections. That's a warning sign, not an advantage.

The cost of time: financing fees

With leverage, the broker is effectively lending you the difference. If you hold the position overnight, you pay interest on the exposure. Example (fictional): a financing rate of 6% a year on €10,000 of exposure, i.e. 10,000 × 6% / 365 ≈ €1.64 per night, about €49 over 30 nights. For a swing trader who holds positions for weeks, this cost matters.

Hidden leverage: the real question is size

Leverage itself is just a tool. What ruins accounts is committing too much relative to your capital. A trader with €10,000 who opens a €10,000 CFD position (effective leverage of 1) takes the same risk as buying the shares. A trader with €1,000 who opens €10,000 takes ten times more risk.

In module 4, you'll learn to set your position size based on the loss you're willing to accept (the famous 1% rule), not on the maximum leverage the platform offers. For now, remember this: the maximum leverage allowed is never a recommendation. It's one of the main reasons why 70 to 90% of CFD accounts lose money.

Key takeaways

  • Long position: you win if the price rises; your loss is limited to your stake.
  • Short selling: you sell borrowed shares to buy them back cheaper. Limited gain, theoretically unlimited loss.
  • A short squeeze is a violent rise caused by short sellers forced to buy back.
  • Leverage: exposure = margin × leverage. It multiplies gains, losses and fees.
  • For retail CFDs in Europe: liquidation at 50% of the required margin, negative balance protection, capped leverage (30 on major currencies, 5 on shares, 2 on crypto).
  • Holding a leveraged position overnight costs financing fees.
  • The danger isn't leverage itself, but a position size too large for your capital.

Exercise

  1. You short 100 shares at €40. Calculate your result if you buy back at €34, then if you buy back at €49.
  2. You have €2,000. You buy a CFD on a share for an exposure of €5,000, with leverage of 5. How much margin is locked up? The share falls 10%: how much do you lose, and what percentage of your account is that?
  3. You have €1,500. You open a CFD on a major index for an exposure of €20,000 with leverage of 20. What's the required margin? With the liquidation rule at 50% of margin, how far (in %) must the index fall for your position to be closed automatically?
  4. You hold this €20,000 position for 20 nights, with a financing rate of 5% a year. How much does the financing cost you?
  5. Food for thought: why do we say that a short sale without a stop is more dangerous than a purchase without a stop?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Buy back at €34: 100 × (40 − 34) = +€600. Buy back at €49: 100 × (40 − 49) = −€900. A 22.5% rise costs you more than a 15% fall would have earned you.
  2. Margin: 5,000 / 5 = €1,000. Loss: 5,000 × 10% = €500, i.e. 500 / 2,000 = 25% of your account, for a 10% move in the share. That's effective leverage of 2.5 on your capital (5,000 / 2,000).
  3. Required margin: 20,000 / 20 = €1,000. Liquidation when the account is worth 50% × 1,000 = €500, so after a loss of 1,500 − 500 = €1,000. Fall needed: 1,000 / 20,000 = 5%. An index can lose 5% in one or two choppy sessions: this account is in permanent danger.
  4. 20,000 × 5% / 365 × 20 ≈ €54.79, about 3.7% of your €1,500 capital, just for holding the position for three weeks.
  5. When buying, the worst case is known: the share goes to zero and you lose your stake. With a short, there's no ceiling: the price can double, triple, and every euro of rise is a euro of loss per share. On top of that, sharp rises (short squeeze, takeover bid, surprise good news) often come as gaps, leaving you no time to react. A stop is therefore essential when short, even if it doesn't protect perfectly against gaps.

Next lesson: we open module 2 and learn to read a chart, starting with Japanese candlesticks.

7.html:
Why it matters

Welcome to module 2. So far, we've talked about markets, orders and fees. Now we open the chart. On almost every platform, the default chart is a Japanese candlestick chart. A single candle summarises what happened during a period: where the price started, where it finished, how high and how low it went. And above all, it tells you which side, buyers or sellers, won the battle (remember lesson 3: the price moves according to who's in more of a hurry). Knowing how to read a candle is the alphabet for the rest of the course.

The four prices of a candle

Each candle represents a fixed period (a day, an hour, five minutes; we'll look at this in lesson 8). It's built from four prices, often written OHLC:

  • O (open): the opening price, the first trade of the period;
  • H (high): the highest price reached;
  • L (low): the lowest price reached;
  • C (close): the closing price, the last trade of the period.

The body and the wicks

  • The body is the rectangle between the open and the close.
  • The wicks (or shadows) are the thin lines above and below the body. They extend to the high and the low.

The colour

  • Bullish candle: the close is above the open. It's usually green (or white).
  • Bearish candle: the close is below the open. It's usually red (or black).

Body = |close − open|

Upper wick = high − max(open, close)

Lower wick = min(open, close) − low

Range = high − low

Example (fictional): a share opens at €100, climbs to €104, drops to €99, closes at €103. A bullish candle, with a €3 body, a €1 upper wick, a €1 lower wick and a €5 range. The body makes up 60% of the range: buyers dominated the session from start to finish, without being pushed around too much.

What a candle tells you

Read each candle as a little match between buyers and sellers:

  • A big body (the body takes up most of the range): one side dominated from start to finish. A big green candle shows very determined buyers.
  • A small body: the period ended almost where it started. Nobody really won: indecision.
  • A long lower wick: at some point, sellers pushed the price down, then buyers pushed it back up. The low prices were rejected.
  • A long upper wick: buyers pushed, then sellers took back control. The high prices were rejected.

A candle shows the result, not the whole film: it doesn't tell you in what order the high and low were reached. For that, you need to zoom in on a smaller timeframe (lesson 8).

Single-candle patterns

The doji: indecision

A doji has an almost non-existent body: the open and the close are at nearly the same level. Example: open €45.10, high €45.80, low €44.40, close €45.12. A €0.02 body for a €1.40 range. Both sides fought and ended up back where they started. After a long rise, a doji can signal that buyers are running out of steam.

The hammer: rejection of low prices

A hammer has a small body at the top of the candle and a long lower wick, at least twice the size of the body, with little or no upper wick. Example: open €50.00, high €50.60, low €48.20, close €50.50. Body €0.50, lower wick €1.80 (3.6 times the body), upper wick €0.10. Sellers made the price plunge, then buyers took it all back. After a fall, it's a possible sign of an upward reversal. The same shape after a rise is called a hanging man and is read more as a warning.

The shooting star: rejection of high prices

It's the upside-down hammer: small body at the bottom, long upper wick. Example: open €80.40, high €82.40, low €79.90, close €80.00. An upper wick of €2, i.e. 5 times the body (€0.40). After a rise, buyers tried to push higher and were pushed back: a possible sign of exhaustion.

Two-candle patterns: the engulfing

An engulfing pattern occurs when a candle's body completely covers the body of the previous candle, in the opposite colour.

DayOpenCloseColour
Day 1€30.00€29.20bearish
Day 2€29.00€30.40bullish

Day 2's body (from €29.00 to €30.40) completely covers day 1's (from €29.20 to €30.00). That's a bullish engulfing: sellers were in charge, then buyers not only wiped out the previous day but closed above it. It carries more weight after a fall. The bearish engulfing is the mirror image, after a rise.

Context matters more than the pattern

This is beginners' number one mistake: seeing a hammer and buying. A candlestick pattern on its own has weak predictive power. It becomes interesting when it appears in the right place:

  • after a clear move (a hammer in the middle of a directionless market means almost nothing);
  • on an important level, such as support or resistance (lesson 10);
  • with high volume confirming the interest of buyers or sellers (lesson 12);
  • on a large enough timeframe: a daily candle carries more weight than a 5-minute candle.

Remember too that a candle is only finished at the close of its period. A lovely hammer at 15:00 can turn into a big red candle by 17:30. Never judge a candle that's still forming.

And even in the right place, a pattern is often wrong. That's why it's used to prepare a decision, never as an excuse to skip a stop.

Key takeaways

  • A candle summarises a period with 4 prices: open, high, low, close (OHLC).
  • Green if the close is above the open, red otherwise.
  • Big body = one side dominated. Small body = indecision. Long wick = prices rejected.
  • Doji (indecision), hammer (lows rejected), shooting star (highs rejected), engulfing (one side abruptly takes back control).
  • A pattern on its own predicts little: it's the context (trend, level, volume) that gives it meaning.
  • Only judge a candle once it has closed.

Exercise

  1. A candle: open €62.00, high €63.50, low €61.40, close €62.90. Is it bullish or bearish? Calculate the body, both wicks and the range.
  2. Identify each candle:
    1. O €20.00; H €21.00; L €19.00; C €20.02
    2. O €34.60; H €35.20; L €33.20; C €35.10
    3. O €70.00; H €70.10; L €66.00; C €66.20
  3. Here are four consecutive candles covering a whole day. Rebuild the daily candle (O, H, L, C) and describe it.
    CandleOHLC
    110.0010.309.9010.20
    210.2010.6010.1010.50
    310.5010.559.709.80
    49.8010.159.7510.10
  4. After two weeks of decline, you see: day 1, O €48.00 and C €47.10; day 2, O €46.95 and C €48.50. Which pattern do you recognise? Explain why.
  5. Food for thought: your friend sees a hammer on a 5-minute chart, in the middle of a directionless day, and wants to buy immediately. What do you tell him?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Close (€62.90) above open (€62.00): bullish candle. Body = 62.90 − 62.00 = €0.90. Upper wick = 63.50 − 62.90 = €0.60. Lower wick = 62.00 − 61.40 = €0.60. Range = 63.50 − 61.40 = €2.10. The body is about 43% of the range: an edge to buyers, but a contested session.
  2. a) A €0.02 body for a €2 range: doji, total indecision. b) €0.50 body, €1.40 lower wick (2.8 times the body), €0.10 upper wick: hammer (low prices rejected). c) A €3.80 body over a €4.10 range (about 93%): big bearish candle, sellers dominated the whole period and closed near the low.
  3. Open = the first candle's: €10.00. High = the highest of the highs: €10.60. Low = the lowest of the lows: €9.70. Close = the last one's: €10.10. The daily candle is slightly bullish, with a tiny body (€0.10) for a €0.90 range: a day of indecision. Yet in detail there was a real rise and then a real drop. Same market, two readings depending on the timeframe: that's the subject of the next lesson.
  4. Day 1 bearish (body from €47.10 to €48.00), day 2 bullish with a body (from €46.95 to €48.50) that completely covers day 1's. It's a bullish engulfing, and it appears after a fall, which gives it more weight. That still doesn't make it an automatic buy signal: you'd need to look at the level where it forms and at the volume.
  5. A hammer on a 5-minute chart, with no prior trend and no important level, has almost no value: dozens of them appear every day, at random. A candlestick pattern is only worth something in its context (prior move, support, volume, timeframe). And even in a good context, you need a plan: where to enter, where to put the stop, how much to risk.

Next lesson: timeframes and multi-timeframe analysis, or how the same market can be rising and falling at the same time.

8.html:
The same market can be rising and falling at the same time

At the end of lesson 7, you rebuilt a daily candle from four shorter candles: in detail, a real rise and then a real drop; seen from afar, a day of indecision. That's no accident, it's a fundamental property of markets. Depending on the timeframe you look at, the same share can be rising, falling or going nowhere. Many beginners lose money because they analyse on one chart and trade on another without realising it. This lesson teaches you how to choose your timeframes and combine them.

What is a timeframe?

The timeframe is the period represented by each candle on the chart. Platforms use abbreviations:

AbbreviationOne candle =Typical use
M1, M51 or 5 minutesscalping
M15, M3015 or 30 minutesday trading
H1, H41 or 4 hoursday trading, fine-tuning a swing entry
D11 dayswing trading
W11 weekswing and position trading
MN1 monthlong-term view, investing

A quick calculation to fix ideas. A session on Euronext runs from 9:00 to 17:30, i.e. 510 minutes. So it contains 102 M5 candles, 34 M15 candles, and 9 H1 candles (the last one lasts only half an hour). On forex, open 24 hours a day on weekdays, a week has 5 × 24 = 120 H1 candles.

A small trap: the forex "daily" candle

For a share, the day runs from the exchange's open to its close. In forex, which doesn't close overnight, a cut-off time has to be chosen, and it varies between brokers (often 17:00 in New York, i.e. 23:00 in Paris for most of the year). Two platforms can therefore show slightly different daily candles for the same pair.

The smaller the timeframe, the more noise dominates

On an M5 chart, each candle reacts to a single big order, an algorithm, a rumour. These moves are largely random: that's what we call noise. The higher you go in timeframe, the more these little accidents cancel out, and the more the underlying moves (trends, key levels) become readable.

This has two very concrete consequences.

1. Fees weigh more heavily on small timeframes

Example (fictional): a share at €50, with a round-trip cost (commission + spread) of about 0.1%, i.e. €0.05 per share.

  • On M5, a realistic target is around €0.30: fees eat 0.05 / 0.30 ≈ 17% of the expected gain.
  • On D1, a realistic target is around €3: fees eat only 0.05 / 3 ≈ 1.7% of the expected gain.

It's the same observation as in lesson 1: the shorter it is, the more fees are an opponent.

2. Tight stops get "hunted"

If the €50 share regularly moves €2 in a day, a stop placed €0.30 below your purchase price is very likely to be hit by noise alone, even if your idea was good. The timeframe and the stop distance must be consistent: we'll measure this properly with the ATR in lesson 16.

Each timeframe has its own trend

Imagine a (fictional) share on three charts:

TimeframeWhat you see
W1 (weekly)steady rise for a year, from €40 to €60
D1 (daily)pullback for two weeks, from €60 to €55
H1 (hourly)since yesterday, the price has bounced from €55 to €56

Is the share rising or falling? All three at once, depending on the scale. The daily pullback is just a small wave inside the big weekly tide, and the hourly bounce is just a ripple inside the pullback. All three readings are true. The question isn't "which one is right?" but "what is each one for in my decision?".

Multi-timeframe analysis: top down

The classic method is to use three timeframes, each with a specific role, always starting from the largest:

  1. The long timeframe: the context. Which way is the tide going? Where are the big levels?
  2. The main timeframe: the decision. This is the one where you look for opportunities and manage your position.
  3. The short timeframe: the timing. It's used to fine-tune the entry and place the stop more precisely.

Rule of thumb: a factor of about 4 to 8 between two successive timeframes.

Examples: W1 → D1 → H4 (swing trading); H4 → H1 → M15 (day trading).

Example analysis (fictional)

Let's go back to our share, for a swing trader whose main timeframe is D1.

  • W1: clear uptrend. A context that favours buying; we avoid shorting.
  • D1: pullback from €60 towards €55, an area where the price had already bounced several times (we'll talk about support in lesson 10). The pullback is slowing. It's a situation to watch for a buy.
  • H1: a hammer then a bullish engulfing around €55, and the price heads back up. That's a possible trigger, with a stop below the recent low.

All three timeframes point the same way: this is what traders call alignment. There's no certainty, but you're buying with the tide, just as the wave restarts, with a defined risk.

When timeframes contradict each other

If W1 is bearish and H1 gives you a buy signal, you're swimming against the current. It isn't forbidden, but it's riskier, and a beginner would do well to stay out. Doing nothing is a trading decision in its own right.

Choosing your timeframes

The choice depends first on your timetable (lesson 2) and your style (lesson 1):

  • You're in class during the day and analyse in the evening: D1 as your main timeframe, W1 for context, H4 or H1 to fine-tune. That's the realistic framework for a student, and the one in our examples.
  • Once chosen, don't switch timeframes mid-trade. The classic trap: entering on a D1 signal, then panicking while watching M5 and closing the position on a move that's just noise at the scale of your analysis. Or the reverse: entering on an M5 signal and, when it goes wrong, "switching to D1" to convince yourself to hold a losing position.

Remember too that, across all timeframes, most retail traders lose money. Choosing a longer timeframe doesn't make you a winner, but it reduces the weight of fees, noise and decisions made in the heat of the moment.

Key takeaways

  • The timeframe is the duration of one candle: M5, H1, D1, W1...
  • The smaller the timeframe, the more noise and fees weigh, and the more tight stops get hit at random.
  • The same market can be bullish on W1, bearish on D1 and bullish on H1: all these readings are true.
  • Analyse top down: long (context), main (decision), short (timing), with a factor of about 4 to 8.
  • The best situations are those where the timeframes are aligned. When they contradict, staying out is a valid choice.
  • For a student: D1 as the main timeframe, analysed in the evening.
  • Never switch timeframes during a trade.

Exercise

  1. How many M15 candles are there in a full Euronext session (9:00 – 17:30)? How many H4 candles in a forex week (Sunday evening to Friday evening, 5 × 24 hours)?
  2. Can a daily candle be bullish while most of its H1 candles are bearish? Explain with a simple example.
  3. Your round-trip cost is €0.08 per share. On M5, you aim for €0.20 of gain per trade; on D1, you aim for €4. What share of the expected gain do fees represent in each case?
  4. Put these three timeframes in the order of a multi-timeframe analysis for a swing trader, and give the role of each: H4, W1, D1.
  5. Food for thought: on W1, the CAC 40 has been clearly falling for six months. On H1, you spot a nice buy signal. What do you do, and why?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. 510 minutes / 15 = 34 M15 candles. For forex: 5 × 24 = 120 hours, i.e. 120 / 4 = 30 H4 candles.
  2. Yes. Example: the day opens at €100, a single H1 candle rises sharply from €100 to €104, then the next eight drift slightly lower to €102. Most H1 candles are red, but the close (€102) is above the open (€100): the daily candle is green. Counting candles isn't enough; it's the size of the moves that counts.
  3. On M5: 0.08 / 0.20 = 40% of the expected gain goes on fees. On D1: 0.08 / 4 = 2%. To be profitable on M5, you need a far better strategy, just to make up for the fees.
  4. W1 (context: direction of the underlying trend, big levels), then D1 (decision: spotting the opportunity and managing the position), then H4 (timing: fine-tuning the entry and the stop).
  5. The H1 signal goes against the underlying trend. The most prudent thing, especially as a beginner, is not to take it, or at the very least to wait until the intermediate timeframe (D1) also shows a reversal. An hourly bounce in a weekly decline is often just a ripple before the decline resumes. If you take it anyway, it must be with a strict stop and a reduced size.

Next lesson: the trend. How to define it objectively with highs and lows, and spot the moment it breaks.

9.html:
Why it matters

"The trend is your friend." It's probably the most repeated saying in trading, and one of the most useful. But saying "it's going up" while looking at a chart isn't enough: we often see what we want to see. You need an objective definition, the same for everyone, that lets you say at any given moment: the trend is up, down, or there isn't one. And above all, that lets you spot the moment it breaks. This definition rests on a very simple concept: highs and lows.

Highs and lows

The price never rises in a straight line. It moves in waves: it rises, pulls back, rises again, pulls back again. Each wave leaves two traces on the chart:

  • a high (swing high): a peak, from which the price came back down;
  • a low (swing low): a trough, from which the price came back up.

A simple rule for spotting them on candles: a swing high is a candle whose high is above those of the two candles to its left and the two candles to its right. For a swing low, it's the same with the lows. So you can only confirm a high or a low after the fact, once the following candles have formed.

The three states of the market

Uptrend = higher and higher highs AND higher and higher lows.

Downtrend = lower and lower highs AND lower and lower lows.

Range (trendless market) = highs and lows at roughly the same level.

This definition comes from Dow theory, formulated by Charles Dow (one of the founders of the Wall Street Journal) at the end of the 19th century. It's more than a century old, and it's still the basis of almost all technical analysis.

StateHighsLowsWhat it means
Bullishhigher and higherhigher and higherbuyers come back in at ever higher prices
Bearishlower and lowerlower and lowersellers accept ever lower prices
Rangeat the same levelat the same levelbalance: nobody gets the upper hand

Markets spend a lot of their time in ranges. That's important to know: trend strategies (lesson 25) lose money when there's no trend, and mean-reversion strategies (lesson 27) lose money when a strong trend sets in.

Impulses and corrections

In a trend, there are two kinds of waves:

  • impulses, which go in the direction of the trend;
  • corrections (or pullbacks), which go against it.

In a healthy trend, impulses are larger (and often faster) than corrections. The depth of a correction is often measured as a percentage of the previous impulse:

Retracement = size of the correction / size of the previous impulse

A retracement of 30 to 60% is common in a trend. When corrections become deeper than impulses, the trend is running out of steam. We'll come back to the most-watched retracement levels in lesson 18.

Full example: the life of a trend (fictional)

Here are a share's successive highs and lows, on a daily chart:

PointTypePriceReading
Alow€100starting point
Bhigh€110impulse of +€10
Clow€104low higher than A: the uptrend is taking shape
Dhigh€116high higher than B: uptrend confirmed
Elow€109low higher than C: the trend continues
Fhigh€114high lower than D: first warning
Glow€102goes below low E (€109): uptrend broken

A few calculations:

  • Impulse A → B: +€10. Correction B → C: −€6, a retracement of 6 / 10 = 60%.
  • Impulse C → D: +€12. Correction D → E: −€7, i.e. 7 / 12 ≈ 58%.
  • Then impulse E → F only manages +€5 and fails to get past D. Correction F → G is −€12, more than double the impulse. The balance of power has flipped.

The key moment: breaking the last low

The lower high at F is a warning, not yet a break: buyers lacked strength, but the structure (higher and higher lows) still holds. The uptrend is officially broken when the price goes below the last low (E, €109). From there, you have a lower high and a lower low: it may be the start of a downtrend, or of a range. A new lower high will be needed to confirm a downtrend.

For a buyer, the last low is therefore a logical level for a stop: if the price goes below it, the very reason for the trade (the uptrend) has disappeared.

Close or wick?

The price sometimes dips below a low for the length of a wick, then bounces straight back. Many traders wait for a close below the level (on D1, a daily close) before considering the break valid. There's no universal rule, but you need to pick yours and always apply it the same way.

Using the trend to trade

  • Trade in the direction of the trend on your main timeframe, and if possible on the higher timeframe too (lesson 8).
  • In an uptrend, look to buy during corrections, near a potential low, rather than after a big green candle: the stop (below the last low) is closer, so the risk is smaller.
  • Don't try to guess the final high or low: "buy at the bottom, sell at the top" is a fantasy. Settle for the middle of the move.
  • When the structure breaks, don't cling on: the trend your trade was based on no longer exists.

None of this is a guarantee. A trend can reverse without warning, on a piece of news. But the structure of highs and lows gives you a framework: a direction to trade in, and a logical place to admit you were wrong.

Key takeaways

  • The price moves in waves, which leave highs and lows.
  • Uptrend = higher highs and higher lows. Downtrend = lower highs and lower lows. Range = roughly stable levels.
  • In a healthy trend, impulses are larger than corrections. Retracement = correction / impulse.
  • A lower high (in an uptrend) is a warning; breaking the last low breaks the trend.
  • The last low is a logical place for a buyer's stop.
  • Buy the corrections in an uptrend rather than the big euphoric candles.

Exercise

  1. Here are sequences of successive highs and lows. For each, say whether the trend is up, down or ranging.
    1. Low 50, high 55, low 52, high 58, low 54, high 61.
    2. High 80, low 74, high 77, low 70, high 73, low 66.
    3. Low 30, high 34, low 30.50, high 33.80, low 30.20, high 34.10.
  2. A share rises from €40 to €52, then corrects to €46. What's the retracement as a percentage?
  3. An uptrend sequence: low €20, high €25, low €22, high €28, low €24.50, high €27. Which point is a first warning? At what price will the uptrend be broken? Where would a buyer logically put their stop?
  4. In a downtrend: high €80, low €72, high €76, low €66. Calculate the two falls as percentages (80 → 72 and 76 → 66) and the retracement of the 72 → 76 correction.
  5. Food for thought: in an uptrend, why is it generally better to buy during a correction rather than just after a big green candle?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. a) Lows 50 → 52 → 54 and highs 55 → 58 → 61, all higher and higher: uptrend. b) Highs 80 → 77 → 73 and lows 74 → 70 → 66, all lower and lower: downtrend. c) Lows around 30 and highs around 34, with no clear progression: a range between about €30 and €34.
  2. Impulse: 52 − 40 = €12. Correction: 52 − 46 = €6. Retracement: 6 / 12 = 50%, a classic correction within a trend.
  3. The high at €27 is lower than the previous one (€28): that's the first warning. The uptrend will be broken if the price goes below €24.50, the last low (ideally confirmed by a close). A buyer would put their stop a little below €24.50 (for example €24.30), to leave a small margin against noise.
  4. Fall 80 → 72: 8 / 80 = −10%. Fall 76 → 66: 10 / 76 ≈ −13.2%. Correction 72 → 76: €4 on a downward impulse of €8, a retracement of 50%. The second impulse is bigger than the first: the downtrend is vigorous.
  5. During a correction, the price is close to the last low, so your stop (below that low) is close: the risk per share is small, and the upside potential to the next high is large. After a big green candle, you're buying far from the last low: either your stop is very far away (high risk), or you put it too close and noise hits it. On top of that, buying after a strong rise often means buying on a wave of enthusiasm (we'll talk about FOMO in lesson 35).

Next lesson: support and resistance, those price zones where buyers and sellers habitually do battle.

10.html:
Why it matters

Open any chart covering several months: you'll see that the price seems to "bounce" off certain levels, and "stall" under others, again and again. It isn't magic, it's collective memory. Support and resistance are the zones where buyers and sellers have already clashed, and where they're likely to meet again. They're also the most useful markers for deciding where to enter, where to put your stop and where to take your profits. If you remember only one tool from the whole of module 2, it should probably be this one.

Definitions
