  • They cut their losses quickly and let their gains run: an average gain bigger than the average loss (lesson 22).
  • They have a written, tested plan (lessons 24 and 28), and a trading journal (lesson 29).
  • They trade less, but better, and keep their costs low.
  • They accept that losing is part of the job, and focus on the process rather than on the outcome of any single trade.

And a perfectly honourable option: deciding, after learning all this, that active trading isn't for you and favouring long-term investing. Understanding why people lose also means knowing when not to play.

Key takeaways

  • The vast majority of retail traders lose money: between 70 and 90% on CFDs according to mandatory disclosures, and even more among day traders who persist.
  • Costs turn a zero-sum game into a losing one, especially when you trade often.
  • Asymmetry: losing 50% means you need to gain 100% to break even.
  • Leverage accelerates losses as much as gains.
  • The disposition effect (cutting gains, holding losses) makes a strategy that often wins into a losing one.
  • Without an edge, without a plan and with unrealistic goals, the odds are against you.
  • The answer is risk management: the subject of lessons 20 to 23.

Exercise

  1. A trader loses 25% of their capital. What gain do they need to break even? And after a 40% loss?
  2. Your account loses 40%, then gains 40%. Are you back where you started? Calculate your final result as a percentage.
  3. Inès has €5,000. She makes 3 round trips a week over 48 weeks, committing €5,000 each time, with 0.15% in fees and spread per round trip. How much do her fees cost her over a year, in euros and as a percentage of her capital?
  4. A trader wins only 40% of their trades, but their average gain is €150 and their average loss €60. Are they winning or losing on average per trade? Compare with Sarah.
  5. Food for thought: if 80 to 90% of retail traders lose, does that mean "the remaining 10% just got lucky"? What might distinguish a genuinely skilled trader from a lucky one?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. After −25%: 1 / 0.75 − 1 ≈ +33.3%. After −40%: 1 / 0.60 − 1 ≈ +66.7%.
  2. No. 1 × 0.60 × 1.40 = 0.84: you end up at −16%. The same percentage rise doesn't make up for a fall, because it applies to a smaller base.
  3. Number of round trips: 3 × 48 = 144. Cost: 144 × 5,000 × 0.15% = 144 × 7.50 = €1,080, i.e. 21.6% of her capital. She has to make more than 21% a year just to pay her fees.
  4. Expectancy per trade: 0.40 × 150 − 0.60 × 60 = 60 − 36 = +€24. They're winning on average, even though they lose 6 trades out of 10. Sarah won more often (55%) but lost €10 per trade on average. What counts is the win rate combined with the ratio between average gain and average loss (lesson 22).
  5. Some winners are indeed lucky: out of thousands of traders with no edge, chance will always make a few of them shine for a year or two. What distinguishes a skilled trader is longevity and consistency: positive results over a large number of trades and several years, a written method they can explain and that has been tested, controlled risk (not one big winning bet), a journal showing a coherent process. A single big gain proves nothing; rigorous risk management over time does. You can't control luck, but you can control how much you risk: that's the subject of the next lesson.

Next lesson: risk per trade and the 1% rule. How much to accept losing on a single position, and why this small rule changes everything.

20.html:
Why it matters

Last time, we saw that most traders lose, and that big losses are so hard to recover from (losing 50% means you need to gain 100%). The logical conclusion: a trader's first job isn't to win, it's to survive long enough for any edge they have to show itself. And to survive, you have to decide, before every trade, how much you're willing to lose.

The best-known rule for this fits in one sentence: never risk more than 1% of your capital on a single trade. It seems too cautious, almost boring. We'll see why it's at the heart of almost every professional approach.

Risk isn't the amount invested

This is the most common confusion. "Risking 1%" doesn't mean only buying 1% of your capital's worth. It means: if my stop is hit, I lose 1% of my capital.

Risk of a trade = what you lose if your stop is hit

Maximum risk per trade = capital × risk percentage

Fictional example: you have a €5,000 account. With the 1% rule, your maximum risk per trade is 5,000 × 1% = €50. You can perfectly well buy €1,500 of shares, provided your stop is placed so that you don't lose more than €50 if it's hit. If the share falls 3.3% to your stop, you lose about €50: all good. That's the position-sizing calculation, the subject of lesson 21.

This implies two things:

  • No trade without a stop. Without a stop, your risk isn't 1%: it's undefined, potentially 100% of what you've committed.
  • The stop is decided before getting in, based on the chart (below support, below the last low, at 2 ATR as in lesson 16), not on how much you "feel like" losing.

Why 1%: the law of streaks

Even with a good method, you're going to string losses together. And streaks are far longer than intuition imagines. With a method that wins 40% of the time (common for a trend-following strategy), the probability of having at least one streak of 8 losses in a row over 100 trades is about 49%. One chance in two. With a method that wins 50% of the time, the probability of at least one streak of 6 losses over 100 trades exceeds 54%.

Here's what happens to your capital after 10 losses in a row, depending on the risk taken on each trade (the risk is recalculated on the remaining capital):

Risk per tradeCapital remaining after 10 lossesGain needed to break even
1%90.4%+10.6%
2%81.7%+22.4%
5%59.9%+67.0%
10%34.9%+186.8%

At 1%, a losing streak of 10 is unpleasant but ordinary: less than a 10% fall, easy to recover. At 10%, the same streak leaves you with a third of your account and you'd need to almost triple what's left. The difference between these two traders isn't their talent: it's purely their risk management.

You don't control whether your next trade will win. You control how much it will cost you if it loses.

Proportional risk: an automatic shock absorber

The rule applies to your current capital, not your starting capital. With €5,000 and 1%:

TradeCapital beforeRisk (1%)Capital after a loss
1€5,000.00€50.00€4,950.00
2€4,950.00€49.50€4,900.50
3€4,900.50€49.01€4,851.49

When you lose, your stakes shrink by themselves: you automatically slow down during bad periods. When you win, they grow gently. It's this mechanism that makes total ruin almost impossible as long as you stick to the rule (we'll see this in detail in lesson 23).

1%, 2%, 0.5%: how to choose

  • 0.5% to 1%: the recommended zone for beginners, and the one used by many professionals.
  • 2%: often quoted as a maximum. Beyond that, losing streaks become really painful.
  • Above 2%: you're no longer managing risk, you're gambling.

With a small account, 1% looks paltry: €10 on a €1,000 account. That's exactly the point. A small account is for learning while paying limited "tuition fees", not for getting rich fast. If 1% seems too small to be worth it, that's a sign your profit expectations are too high (lesson 19).

The limits of the rule

  • A stop isn't a guarantee. In the event of a gap (lesson 2) or slippage (lesson 3), your stop order can execute much lower. A "1%" trade can cost 2 or 3% on a gap open after results. That's one more reason to stay small, and to avoid holding positions through major announcements if you don't want that risk.
  • Total risk matters too. Five positions at 1% each is 5% of risk if everything goes wrong at once. And if those five positions are five European banks, they're likely to fall together: in practice, it's almost one big trade. Many traders cap their total open risk, for example at 4 or 5%, and avoid overly correlated positions (lesson 33).
  • A daily or weekly loss limit. For example: if I lose 3% in the week, I stop trading until next Monday. This protects against the "I'll win it back" spiral (lesson 35).

Key takeaways

  • A trade's risk is what you lose if your stop is hit, not the amount invested.
  • The 1% rule: maximum risk per trade = capital × 1% (between 0.5 and 2% depending on the approach).
  • Losing streaks are long and frequent, even with a good method.
  • After 10 losses, you keep about 90% of your capital at 1% risk, only 35% at 10%.
  • Risk is calculated on current capital: stakes shrink by themselves during tough periods.
  • No trade without a stop decided in advance; gaps and slippage can exceed the planned risk.
  • Keep an eye on total open risk and correlated positions too.

Exercise

  1. You have an €8,000 account. What's your maximum risk per trade at 1%? At 0.5%?
  2. With a method that wins 40% of the time, what's the probability that your next 5 trades will all lose?
  3. Two traders start with €10,000 and suffer 20 losses in a row. The first risks 1% per trade, the second 2%. How much capital does each have left?
  4. Your account is worth €6,000. You already have three open positions, each with a risk of €60. You've set yourself a maximum total open risk of 4%. Can you open a fourth position at 1%? And a fifth?
  5. Food for thought: a friend tells you: "With only 1% risk, I'll never make enough for it to change my life, so I'd rather risk 10% per trade." What do you say to him?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. At 1%: 8,000 × 1% = €80. At 0.5%: €40.
  2. Probability of losing a trade: 60%. Five losses in a row: 0.6 to the power of 5 ≈ 7.8%, about one chance in 13. Over a year of trading, it will almost certainly happen at some point.
  3. At 1%: 10,000 × 0.99 to the power of 20 ≈ €8,179 (−18%). At 2%: 10,000 × 0.98 to the power of 20 ≈ €6,676 (−33%). The second needs to gain back about 50% to return to €10,000, the first about 22%.
  4. Maximum total risk: 6,000 × 4% = €240. Already committed: 3 × 60 = €180. A fourth position at 1% (€60) brings the total to €240: exactly the limit, so yes. A fifth would exceed the cap (€300, i.e. 5%): no, you'd have to wait for a position to be closed or for its stop to be moved up to the entry price. And check that the four aren't all tied to the same factor.
  5. With 10% risk, a streak of 10 losses, very likely over a few hundred trades, would leave him with about 35% of his capital, and he'd need nearly +190% to break even. It won't "change his life": he'll very probably lose his account before he's been able to prove anything. Trading doesn't make you rich by betting big; if there's an edge, it's built by surviving over time. And if the possible gains at 1% seem ridiculous to him, it's time to rethink his expectations, or to consider long-term investing instead.

Next lesson: calculating your position size. How to go from "I'm risking €50" to "I'm buying exactly this many shares", for shares, forex and with leverage.

21.html:
Why it matters

Last time, you set your maximum risk: for example 1% of your capital, i.e. €100 on a €10,000 account. But your platform doesn't ask you "how much do you want to risk?". It asks "how many shares do you want to buy?" or "how many lots?". The link between the two is the position size calculation. It's the trader's single most important technical skill, and it only takes one division.

The fundamental principle: it's not conviction that decides the size, it's the distance to the stop. A trade "you're sure about" doesn't deserve a bigger position. A distant stop requires a smaller position.

The basic formula

Risk per unit = |entry price − stop price|

Position size = maximum risk in euros / risk per unit (rounded down to the nearest unit)

Fictional example: you have €10,000 and risk 1%, i.e. €100. You want to buy a share at €50.00, and your analysis puts the stop below support, at €47.50.

  • Risk per share: 50.00 − 47.50 = €2.50.
  • Number of shares: 100 / 2.50 = 40 shares.
  • Amount invested: 40 × 50 = €2,000, i.e. 20% of your capital.

Check: if the stop is hit, you lose 40 × 2.50 = €100, exactly 1%. You've invested €2,000, but you're only risking €100. That's the difference between amount invested and risk seen in lesson 20.

Always round down

If the calculation gives 41.67 shares, you buy 41, never 42. Rounding up means exceeding your risk. On one trade the difference is tiny; over hundreds of trades, it's a habit that counts.

Factoring in fees

To be rigorous, deduct the estimated fees from your risk budget. If the round trip costs you about €4 in commissions, your budget becomes 100 − 4 = €96, and 96 / 2.50 = 38.4, i.e. 38 shares. With low fees the difference is small, but it becomes significant on small accounts and very short trades.

Same risk, different sizes

Let's compare three fictional trades on the same €50 share, still with €100 of risk:

StopRisk per shareNumber of sharesAmount investedLoss if stop hit
€48.00€2.0050€2,500€100
€47.50€2.5040€2,000€100
€45.00€5.0020€1,000€100

The possible loss is identical in all three cases. Only the size adjusts. That's what lets you put your stop where it makes technical sense (below support, below a low), rather than at an arbitrary distance chosen so you "can buy more".

With the ATR

Remember lesson 16: many traders place the stop at a multiple of the ATR. If the ATR is €1.20 and you choose a 2-ATR stop, the risk per share is €2.40, and the size 100 / 2.40 = 41.67, i.e. 41 shares. An elegant result: on a choppy asset, the ATR is large and the position small; on a calm asset, the position is bigger. Every trade carries the same weight in risk, whatever the volatility.

The too-tight stop trap

The formula has a perverse effect: the tighter the stop, the bigger the position. With a stop €0.20 below a €50 entry, you could buy 100 / 0.20 = 500 shares, i.e. €25,000, more than double your capital.

  • Without leverage, it's simply impossible: the size is capped by your available capital.
  • With leverage, it's possible, but dangerous: such a tight stop will often be hit by noise alone, and the slightest gap or slippage (lesson 3) on such a large position will blow up your real risk.

Rule of thumb: if the calculation gives a huge position, the stop is often unrealistic. Check that it's at a distance consistent with volatility (generally at least around one ATR).

In forex and CFDs

The logic is the same; only the units change.

Forex: pips and lots

On EUR/USD, a pip is the fourth decimal place, i.e. 0.0001. Sizes are counted in lots: a standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency (here euros), a mini lot 10,000, a micro lot 1,000. For a standard EUR/USD lot, a pip is worth 10 dollars; for a micro lot, 0.10 dollars.

Size in lots = risk in euros / (stop in pips × value of one pip per lot in euros)

Fictional example: a €5,000 account, 1% risk = €50. Stop at 25 pips. With EUR/USD around 1.08, a pip per standard lot is worth 10 / 1.08 ≈ €9.26. Size: 50 / (25 × 9.26) ≈ 0.216, so 0.21 lots (21 micro lots). Loss if the stop is hit: about 0.21 × 25 × 9.26 ≈ €48.61.

A key point: this position represents 0.21 × 100,000 = €21,000, more than four times your capital. So you're using leverage of about 4. And yet your risk is still 1%. That's how a professional uses leverage: it isn't chosen to make more, it's the consequence of a sizing calculation. The danger comes from those who start from the maximum leverage allowed instead of starting from risk (lesson 6).

Index CFDs

With an index CFD, you often think in euros per point. If you risk €100 with a 40-point stop, your size is 100 / 40 = €2.50 per point. If your broker only accepts sizes in steps, take the step below.

The procedure, step by step

  1. Identify your entry point and your stop from the chart.
  2. Calculate your maximum risk: current capital × risk percentage.
  3. Calculate the risk per unit: entry / stop distance (in euros, pips, points).
  4. Divide, round down, deduct fees if necessary.
  5. Check that the position is compatible with your capital, your total open risk (lesson 20) and the asset's liquidity.
  6. Place the entry order and the stop order at the same time (lesson 4).

Many traders use a small spreadsheet or a position-size calculator. The tool doesn't matter: what matters is never choosing the size "by feel".

Key takeaways

  • Size = risk in euros / (entry − stop), rounded down.
  • It's the distance to the stop that sets the size, not conviction.
  • The stop is placed first according to the chart or the ATR; the size then adjusts.
  • Distant stop = small position; tight stop = big position, capped by capital and common sense.
  • In forex: lots = risk / (pips × pip value per lot). Leverage becomes a consequence of the calculation, not a choice.
  • Factor in fees and check your total open risk before getting in.

Exercise

  1. A €12,000 account, 1% risk. Entry at €84.00, stop at €80.80. How many shares do you buy? What's the amount invested and the exact loss if the stop is hit?
  2. You risk €60 on a share bought at €18.40 with a stop at €17.30. How many shares? What amount invested?
  3. A €4,000 account, 1% risk. A share trades at €25 and its ATR is €0.75. You place your stop 1.5 ATR below the entry. Where's the stop? How many shares do you buy?
  4. A €3,000 account, 1% risk. You want to buy EUR/USD with a 20-pip stop. EUR/USD is about 1.10, and a pip is worth 0.10 dollars per micro lot. How many micro lots can you take? What amount does that represent, and what leverage?
  5. Food for thought: with a €2,000 account and 1% risk, you want to buy a share at €40.00 with a stop at €39.90. Do the calculation. What does the result tell you?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Maximum risk: 12,000 × 1% = €120. Risk per share: 84.00 − 80.80 = €3.20. Size: 120 / 3.20 = 37.5, so 37 shares (rounded down). Amount invested: 37 × 84 = €3,108. Loss if stop hit: 37 × 3.20 = €118.40, just under €120.
  2. Risk per share: 18.40 − 17.30 = €1.10. Size: 60 / 1.10 ≈ 54.5, so 54 shares. Amount invested: 54 × 18.40 = €993.60. Loss if stop hit: 54 × 1.10 = €59.40.
  3. Stop distance: 1.5 × 0.75 = €1.125. Stop at 25 − 1.125 ≈ €23.88 (€23.875, rounded according to the tick size). Maximum risk: €40. Size: 40 / 1.125 ≈ 35.6, so 35 shares, i.e. €875 invested.
  4. Maximum risk: €30. Pip value per micro lot in euros: 0.10 / 1.10 ≈ €0.0909. Risk per micro lot: 20 × 0.0909 ≈ €1.82. Size: 30 / 1.82 ≈ 16.5, so 16 micro lots (0.16 lots), for a loss of about €29.09 if the stop is hit. Amount: 16 × 1,000 = €16,000, i.e. leverage of about 5.3 on a €3,000 account. Yet the risk is still 1%.
  5. Maximum risk: €20. Risk per share: €0.10. Size: 20 / 0.10 = 200 shares, i.e. €8,000: four times your capital. Impossible without leverage, and very dangerous with it. Above all, a 10-cent stop on a €40 share (0.25%) is probably within normal noise: it will be hit without your analysis being wrong. The absurd result of the calculation is an alarm bell: you need to rethink the stop (put it at a technically coherent place, on the scale of the ATR) and accept a smaller position, or give up on the trade.

Next lesson: the risk/reward ratio and expectancy. How to tell whether a strategy can win over time, even while losing more than one trade in two.

22.html:
Being right isn't enough

Since lesson 19, we've been repeating an idea that often shocks beginners: you can lose money while winning 70% of your trades, and make money while losing 60% of them. Today we turn that intuition into a calculation. With two simple tools, the risk/reward ratio and expectancy, you'll be able to say, before even placing an order, whether a strategy has a chance of being profitable over time. It's probably the most important lesson in module 4.

The risk/reward ratio

Remember lessons 20 and 21: before each trade, you set a stop (the price where you admit you were wrong) and deduce your maximum loss from it. You're missing one last piece: the target, the price where you plan to bank your gain.

Risk/reward ratio = (target − entry price) / (entry price − stop)

It's often written "1:2" or "2R": for €1 risked, you aim for €2 of gain.

Example: you buy Schneider Electric shares at €230, stop at €224, target at €245 (illustrative figures). You risk €6 per share to make €15. Ratio: 15 / 6 = 2.5. We say the trade is aiming for 2.5R.

Thinking in "R"

Traders measure their results in R, the unit of risk. 1R is the amount you accept losing on a trade (with the 1% rule from lesson 20 and a €10,000 account, 1R = €100). A trade that ends at the stop is worth −1R. A trade that hits a target at 2.5 times the risk is worth +2.5R.

Why is that handy? Because it makes very different trades comparable: a €20 share, a €400 share, an index, a currency pair. What counts isn't the number of euros or points, but how many times your initial risk you've won or lost.

The win rate you need

The higher your ratio, the less often you need to be right. There's a formula to find a strategy's minimum win rate (its "break-even point"):

Minimum win rate = 1 / (1 + R)

Target ratioMinimum win rate
0.5R (risking 2 to make 1)66.7%
1R50%
1.5R40%
2R33.3%
3R25%

With a ratio of 3, you can be wrong three times out of four and still break even (before fees). With a ratio of 0.5, you need to be right two times out of three just to lose nothing. That's the typical beginner's trap: banking small gains quickly for fear of seeing them vanish, and letting losses run in the hope that "it'll come back".

Expectancy

The ratio alone isn't enough: a ratio of 3 is useless if you only win one trade in ten. What matters is the combination of the two. That's expectancy, the average gain you can expect per trade over a large number of trades.

Expectancy = (win rate × average gain) − (loss rate × average loss)

In R: Expectancy = p × R − (1 − p), where p is the win rate.

If the expectancy is positive, your strategy has an edge. If it's negative, the more you trade, the more you lose, however good you are at picking your moment.

Two traders, two surprises (fictional example)

Trader ATrader B
Win rate40%70%
Average gain€250€60
Average loss€100€150
Expectancy per trade0.4 × 250 − 0.6 × 100 = +€400.7 × 60 − 0.3 × 150 = −€3

Trader B wins 7 trades out of 10 and feels brilliant. Yet over 100 trades, he'll lose about €300. Trader A loses more than one trade in two, lives through frustrating weeks, but makes €40 per trade on average, about €4,000 over 100 trades. The win rate flatters the ego; expectancy fills (or empties) the account.

The table to keep in mind

Expectancy in R by win rate and ratio (before fees):

Win rate1R ratio2R ratio3R ratio
30%−0.4R−0.1R+0.2R
40%−0.2R+0.2R+0.6R
50%0+0.5R+1.0R
60%+0.2R+0.8R+1.4R

An expectancy of +0.2R to +0.5R per trade is already very good in real life. Be wary of anyone promising you much more.

The traps in the calculation

Fees nibble away at the edge

Take trader A and add €8 of fees per round trip (commission and spread, see lessons 3 and 5). Each gain drops by €8 and each loss rises by €8: 0.4 × 242 − 0.6 × 108 = +€32. Fees have eaten 20% of his edge. For a trader B or a scalper with tiny gains, they're enough to tip everything into the red.

A target must be realistic

It's easy to write "target 5R" on an order ticket. But if the price almost never reaches that target, your win rate collapses. Ratio and win rate are linked: the further away the target, the less often it's hit. A good target is based on the chart, for example the next resistance (lesson 10), not on a round number chosen because it looks nice.

Expectancy only shows over time

Expectancy is an average over many trades. Over 10 trades, chance dominates: a good strategy can lose, a bad one can win. It's like a coin: over 10 tosses you can get 7 heads without the coin being rigged. You need dozens, ideally more than 100 trades, to start judging. We'll come back to this in lesson 28 (backtesting) and lesson 29 (the trading journal).

The real average gain isn't the target gain

In real life, you sometimes exit before the target, suffer slippage at the stop (lesson 3), or a gap jumps over your stop (lesson 2). To calculate your expectancy, use your real results (actual average gain and average loss), not the figures you were hoping for.

Key takeaways

  • Risk/reward ratio = target gain / accepted loss. It's expressed in R: 1R = the amount risked on a trade.
  • Minimum win rate = 1 / (1 + R): 50% at 1R, 33.3% at 2R, 25% at 3R.
  • Expectancy = p × average gain − (1 − p) × average loss. It must be positive, otherwise trading more just means losing more.
  • A high win rate guarantees nothing: 70% winning trades can give a negative expectancy.
  • Fees reduce expectancy on every trade; they're deadly for small gains.
  • Expectancy can only be judged over a large number of trades, with real results.

Exercise

  1. You buy a share at €50, with a stop at €48 and a target at €56. What's the risk/reward ratio? What minimum win rate do you need to break even?
  2. A strategy wins 45% of its trades with an average ratio of 2R. Calculate its expectancy in R. With 1R = €100, how much can you hope to make over 50 trades (before fees)?
  3. A trader wins 55% of their trades, with an average gain of €80 and an average loss of €120. Calculate their expectancy. What average gain would they need, at minimum, to break even?
  4. Take the strategy from question 2 with 1R = €100. Each trade costs €10 in fees (added to losses, deducted from gains). What's the new expectancy per trade in euros?
  5. Food for thought: a friend tells you: "I always aim for 5R, so I only need to be right one time in six." What do you think?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Risk: 50 − 48 = €2 per share. Target gain: 56 − 50 = €6. Ratio: 6 / 2 = 3R. Minimum win rate: 1 / (1 + 3) = 25%.
  2. Expectancy = 0.45 × 2 − 0.55 × 1 = 0.90 − 0.55 = +0.35R per trade. With 1R = €100, that's €35 per trade, so about €1,750 over 50 trades. Careful: over only 50 trades, the real result can stray quite far from this average.
  3. Expectancy = 0.55 × 80 − 0.45 × 120 = 44 − 54 = −€10 per trade. They win more often than they lose, but lose money. To break even, you need 0.55 × G = 54, i.e. G = 54 / 0.55 ≈ €98.18 average gain (or smaller losses, thanks to respected stops).
  4. Average gain: 200 − 10 = €190. Average loss: 100 + 10 = €110. Expectancy = 0.45 × 190 − 0.55 × 110 = 85.5 − 60.5 = +€25 per trade, versus €35 without fees. Fees have absorbed nearly 30% of the edge.
  5. The calculation is right (1 / (1 + 5) ≈ 16.7%), but the reasoning forgets that ratio and win rate are linked. A target at 5 times the risk is rarely reached: if, in practice, it's only reached one time in ten, the expectancy becomes 0.1 × 5 − 0.9 = −0.4R. On top of that, aiming far means long losing streaks, very hard to bear psychologically (lesson 23). The right ratio isn't the biggest possible one, it's the one the market allows you to reach often enough, which only a test on real data can tell you.

Next lesson: drawdown, losing streaks and risk of ruin. Why a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to get back to zero, and how to survive the bad patches.

23.html:
Why it matters

In lesson 22, we saw that a positive-expectancy strategy makes money "on average, over many trades". The problem is the word "many". In the meantime, there'll be weeks when nothing works, streaks of five, eight, ten losses in a row. If your account doesn't survive those stretches, the positive expectancy will never do you any good. This lesson is about survival: measuring the fall, understanding that losing streaks are normal, and avoiding the only irreparable mistake in trading, ruin.

Drawdown: measuring the fall

Drawdown measures how much your account has lost since its last peak.

Drawdown = (account peak − current value) / account peak

The maximum drawdown is the worst fall observed over a period.

Fictional example: Camille starts with €10,000. After three good months, her account reaches €12,000. Then comes a bad patch, and it falls to €9,000. Her drawdown isn't 10% (relative to the start), but (12,000 − 9,000) / 12,000 = 25%, because you always measure from the peak. Psychologically, that's how it feels too: Camille doesn't feel she's lost €1,000, but €3,000.

The painful asymmetry

Here's the most important mathematical fact in this lesson: a percentage loss requires a bigger gain to wipe it out. If you lose 50% of €10,000, you have €5,000 left. To get back to €10,000, you need to make €5,000 on €5,000, i.e. +100%.

Gain needed to get back to the peak = drawdown / (1 − drawdown)

Loss (drawdown)Gain needed to break even
10%11.1%
20%25%
30%42.9%
40%66.7%
50%100%
75%300%
90%900%

Up to 20%, the climb back remains within reach. Beyond 40%, it becomes very difficult. Beyond 50%, it's often the end of the account, and above all of your morale. All of risk management aims to stay at the top of the table.

Losing streaks are normal

The human brain massively underestimates chance. If your strategy wins 40% of the time, you might expect to lose two or three times in a row, no more. In reality, long streaks inevitably happen if you trade long enough.

Probability of experiencing at least one streak of consecutive losses of a certain length, over 100 trades (exact calculation, assuming independent trades):

Length of streakStrategy with 50% win rateStrategy with 40% win rate
5 losses or more81%98%
6 losses or more55%87%
8 losses or more17%49%
10 losses or more4%20%

With a trend-following strategy that wins 40% of the time (we'll see one in lesson 25), you have one chance in two of going through a streak of at least 8 losses in a row in 100 trades. That's not a sign the strategy is broken: it's simply chance. Anyone who doesn't know this abandons a good method at the worst moment, or starts doubling their positions to "win it back".

What the size of the risk changes

Imagine a streak of 10 losses in a row. Each loss is a percentage of the remaining account (fixed-percentage rule, lesson 20):

Risk per tradeLoss after 10 lossesGain needed to recover
1%−9.6%+10.6%
2%−18.3%+22.4%
5%−40.1%+67.0%
10%−65.1%+186.8%

At 1% per trade, a catastrophic streak of 10 losses costs less than 10%: unpleasant, but you recover. At 10% per trade, the same streak leaves a third of the account. It would take nearly 69 losses in a row to lose half the account at 1% per trade, versus 14 at 5% and only 7 at 10%.

Risk of ruin

Risk of ruin is the probability of losing so much that you can't (or won't) carry on. Here, we set "ruin" at a 50% loss of the account.

Take a winning strategy: 40% win rate, 2R ratio, i.e. an expectancy of +0.2R per trade (lesson 22). We used a computer to simulate 20,000 traders applying it over 200 trades, changing only one thing: the risk per trade. Proportion of those who lose at least half their account along the way (orders of magnitude):

Risk per tradeRisk of ruin (−50%) over 200 trades
1%practically zero
2%about 0.1%
5%about 10%
10%about 43%
20%about 83%

The key lesson: a winning strategy can still ruin you if you risk too much per trade. A good expectancy doesn't protect you from bad position sizing.

This is one of the main reasons why most retail traders lose money (lesson 19): many have sound ideas, but stake 10% or 20% of their account per trade, often with leverage (lesson 6). The first normal losing streak knocks them out.

How to survive the bad patches

  • Keep your risk small: 0.5% to 1% per trade when starting out. That's what gives expectancy time to play out.
  • Set circuit breakers: for example, stop trading for the day after −2%, for the week after −4%, and take a complete break after −10% to analyse what's going wrong.
  • Reduce size in drawdown, never increase it to "win it back". Some traders halve their risk as long as they're more than 10% below their peak.
  • Know your strategy's expected drawdown in advance (thanks to the backtest in lesson 28). A 12% fall won't panic you if you know it's within the norm.
  • Watch your total open risk: five positions at 1% on shares that move together is almost a single 5% bet.

Key takeaways

  • Drawdown is measured from the account's peak, not from the starting capital.
  • Losses are asymmetric: −50% requires +100% to break even.
  • Long losing streaks are statistically normal: at a 40% win rate, a streak of 8 losses in 100 trades happens one time in two.
  • At 1% risk per trade, 10 losses in a row cost less than 10%; at 10%, they cost nearly two thirds of the account.
  • A winning strategy can ruin a trader who risks too much per trade.
  • Small risk, circuit breakers and reducing size in drawdown are your life insurance.

Exercise

  1. Your account goes from a peak of €12,000 to €9,000. What's your drawdown? What percentage gain do you need to get back to €12,000?
  2. With a €5,000 account and a risk of 2% of the remaining account per trade, what's your account worth after 8 losses in a row? How much have you lost?
  3. Your strategy wins 35% of its trades. What's the probability that the next 5 trades will all be losers? Given that the probability of at least one streak of 8 losses in 100 trades is about 69%, what should you conclude?
  4. How many consecutive losses does it take to lose 30% of the account with a risk of 3% per trade? And with 1%?
  5. Food for thought: after a losing streak, your account is at −15%. You think: "If I double my position size, I'll recover twice as fast." Why is that a bad idea?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Drawdown = (12,000 − 9,000) / 12,000 = 25%. Gain needed: 3,000 / 9,000 ≈ 33.3% (or 0.25 / 0.75). Much more than the 25% lost.
  2. Each loss leaves 98% of the remaining account, so 5,000 × 0.98 to the power of 8 ≈ €4,253.82. Loss: about €746.18, i.e. 14.9%. A bit less than 8 × 2% = 16%, because each loss applies to a smaller account.
  3. 0.65 to the power of 5 ≈ 0.116, i.e. about 11.6%: roughly one chance in nine, nothing exceptional. And a streak of 8 losses is more likely than not over 100 trades. Conclusion: you need to size your risk so you can withstand without panicking at least 8 to 10 losses in a row, and decide this before they happen.
  4. We look for n such that 0.97 to the power of n ≤ 0.70. We get n ≈ 11.7, so 12 losses at 3%. At 1%, you need 0.99 to the power of n ≤ 0.70, i.e. n ≈ 35.5, so 36 losses. Dividing the risk by 3 triples the number of losses you can absorb.
  5. Doubling the size also doubles the losses, at precisely the moment when you're fragile. A new losing streak (entirely possible, see the table) would send the account much lower, into the zone where recovery becomes almost impossible. And psychologically, trading to "win it back" leads to revenge trading (lesson 35). The right reaction is the opposite: reduce the size, check that you're following your plan, and let expectancy do its job.

Next lesson: we open module 5 with the anatomy of a trading plan. Everything you need to write down in black and white before placing a single order.

24.html:
Why write a plan?

Welcome to module 5. You now have tools for reading a chart (modules 2 and 3) and for managing your risk (module 4). All that's left is to put it all together. An airline pilot doesn't decide on their landing procedure while landing: they follow a checklist written in advance, calmly. Traders are the same. When a position moves against you and your heart starts racing, you're in no state to think. The trading plan is the document that decides for you, written when you had a cool head.

Trading plan: a written document that says what to trade, when to enter, when to exit, how much to risk, and what to do when things go wrong.

Without a plan, every decision is improvised, and therefore influenced by the emotion of the moment. Above all, without a plan, it's impossible to know what works: if you do every trade differently, you can't measure any expectancy (lesson 22).

The eight blocks of a plan

1. Your goals and constraints

Why you trade, how much time you can devote to it, what capital you can lose without it changing your life. For a student, the honest answer is often: "to learn, with a small sum, a few hours a week". This block heads off absurd goals like "double my account in three months".

2. The markets you trade

A short list, chosen according to your timetable (lesson 2) and liquidity (lesson 3). For example: "CAC 40 shares and the S&P 500 ETF, nothing else". Limiting yourself lets you get to know how these markets behave.

3. Horizon and timeframes

Your style (lesson 1) and your timeframes (lesson 8): for example "swing trading, trend read on the weekly chart, entries on the daily".

4. The setup: entry conditions

The setup is the precise situation that triggers a trade. It must be clear enough that two people reading it would make the same decision. "It looks like it's going up" isn't a setup. "50-day moving average above the 200, pullback to support, bullish reversal candle" is. Lessons 25 to 27 will give you three classic setups.

5. Exit rules

  • The stop: where it goes (below a low, at a multiple of the ATR...) and the golden rule: you never move it further away.
  • The target: a resistance, a multiple of the risk, or a trailing stop.
  • The time exit: for example, "if nothing has happened in 10 sessions, I get out".

6. Position size and risk limits

This is the heart of module 4: risk per trade (the 1% rule, lesson 20), size calculation (lesson 21), but also overall limits:

  • maximum number of positions open at the same time;
  • maximum total open risk;
  • maximum loss per week or per month, beyond which you stop (the circuit breakers from lesson 23).

7. The routine

When and how you analyse: for example, "on Sunday evening I go through my watchlist; every weekday evening, 20 minutes to check my positions and place my orders". We'll go further in lesson 36.

8. Tracking and review

Every trade is recorded in a journal (lesson 29). Once a month, you take stock: number of trades, win rate, expectancy, adherence to the plan. The plan is only changed at that point, never in the middle of a trade.

A complete example (fictional)

Here's the plan of Léa, a master's student who has €5,000 she can afford to lose.

BlockLéa's plan
GoalLearn over 12 months with controlled risk. No numerical profit target.
MarketsCAC 40 shares only.
HorizonSwing trading, from a few days to 3 weeks. Trend on the weekly, entry on the daily.
SetupUptrend (rising highs and lows), pullback towards the 20-day moving average, bullish candle closing above the previous day's high.
StopBelow the last low. Never moved against her.
Target2R minimum, otherwise no trade.
Risk1% of the account per trade, i.e. €50. Maximum 3 open positions (€150 total risk).
Circuit breakersStop until the following Monday after −3% in the week (€150). A month's break and full review after −6% in the month (€300).
RoutineSunday evening: selection. Every evening: 20 minutes of monitoring, orders placed in advance.
TrackingJournal filled in for every trade, review on the first Sunday of the month.

The plan in action

One evening, Léa spots a share in an uptrend that has pulled back towards its 20-day moving average, then formed a reversal candle. Her plan dictates every number:

  • Entry: €42.00 (a buy stop order above the candle's high, lesson 4).
  • Stop: below the last low, at €40.50. Risk per share: €1.50.
  • Size: 50 / 1.50 = 33.3, rounded down: 33 shares, i.e. €1,386 invested and €49.50 of actual risk.
  • Target at 2R: 42.00 + 2 × 1.50 = €45.00. There's resistance around €45.50, so the target is realistic.

Léa didn't ask herself whether she had a "feeling" about the trade. She ticked boxes. If the resistance had been at €43, the trade wouldn't have offered 2R: she'd have let it go, even reluctantly.

The qualities of a good plan

  • Written: a plan in your head changes its mind according to your mood.
  • Precise: every rule can be checked with a yes or a no.
  • Short: one or two pages. A thirty-page plan will never be reread.
  • Tested: before putting money on it, the setup is tested on the past (lesson 28) and in paper trading (lesson 29).
  • Suited to you: copying a professional day trader's plan when you're in class all day won't work.
  • Stable: it's reviewed on fixed dates, based on data, not after every loss.

And keep in mind the reality from lesson 19: most retail traders lose money. A plan doesn't guarantee you'll win. It guarantees your losses will be limited and understandable, which is the condition for making progress.

Key takeaways

  • The trading plan is written in cold blood to decide for you when emotions run high.
  • It contains: goals, markets, horizon, entry setup, exit rules, size and risk limits, routine, tracking.
  • A setup must be precise enough that two people would make the same decision.
  • Circuit breakers (maximum loss per week or month) are part of the plan.
  • A trade that doesn't tick every box isn't taken.
  • The plan is reviewed on fixed dates, based on the journal, never in the middle of a trade.

Exercise

  1. A friend shows you his "plan": "I buy shares that are going up and sell when I've made enough." Name at least four essential elements that are missing.
  2. Apply Léa's plan (€5,000 account, 1% risk): entry at €18.40, stop below the last low at €17.60. How many shares does she buy, how much does she invest, and where does she put her 2R target?
  3. Léa already has 3 open positions. A new perfect setup appears on another share. What does her plan say?
  4. This week, Léa has lost three trades of €50 each. It's Wednesday evening and a setup appears. What does she do?
  5. Food for thought: why is it dangerous to change your plan right after a losing streak, even if you think you're improving it?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Missing, among other things: the list of markets; a precise setup ("going up" since when, on what timeframe?); a stop (nothing is planned if the share falls); a defined target ("enough" isn't a number); the position size and risk per trade; overall limits; tracking with a journal. As it stands, it's not a plan, it's a wish.
  2. Risk per share: 18.40 − 17.60 = €0.80. Size: 50 / 0.80 = 62.5, rounded down: 62 shares (actual risk €49.60). Amount invested: 62 × 18.40 = €1,140.80. 2R target: 18.40 + 2 × 0.80 = €20.00, provided no nearby resistance blocks the way.
  3. Her plan limits her to 3 open positions. She doesn't take the trade, even if it's "perfect". She can note it in her journal to see afterwards what it would have done. There will always be other opportunities; there's only one account.
  4. Three losses of €50 make €150, i.e. −3% of the account: the weekly circuit breaker is triggered. She doesn't trade again until Monday. She can use the free time to reread her trades and check she followed her plan.
  5. A losing streak is often normal (lesson 23): changing the rules at that point means reacting to chance, not to a real weakness. You end up jumping from one method to another without ever accumulating enough trades to measure any of them. And the decision is made in a fit of frustration. Better to note down your improvement ideas and examine them at the monthly review, on a sufficient number of trades, and ideally test them first.

Next lesson: strategy 1, trend following. Cutting losses quickly, letting gains run, and accepting being wrong often.

25.html:
"The trend is your friend"

It's probably the most famous saying in the markets. Trend following is the oldest strategy and one of the most studied. The idea is simple: when a price has started to rise (or fall) in a lasting way, it tends to carry on for a while. Rather than predicting reversals, you jump on the moving train and get off when it stops. It's the first of the three strategies in module 5, and the one that best illustrates the module 4 lessons on expectancy.

Why trends exist

If markets were perfectly efficient, any new information would be built into the price instantly, and trends wouldn't last. In practice, several mechanisms prolong them:

  • information spreads slowly: big investors buy in stages over weeks so as not to make the price jump;
  • human behaviour: people first underreact to news, then follow the move for fear of missing the rise;
  • fundamentals change gradually: a cycle of rate rises (lesson 30) or improving company results (lesson 31) plays out over quarters.

Careful: "tending to continue" doesn't mean "certain to continue". Markets also spend a lot of time without a clear trend, in a range (lesson 10). That's where trend following suffers.

The three building blocks of the strategy

1. Identify the trend

You already have all the tools:

  • Highs and lows (lesson 9): higher and higher highs and lows.
  • Moving averages (lesson 13): price above the 50-day moving average, itself above the 200-day.
  • Multi-timeframe (lesson 8): check the trend on the higher timeframe (weekly) before acting on the daily.

2. Enter

Two main families of entries:

  • On a pullback: wait for the price to fall back towards support or a moving average, then head up again. You get in at a better price, but sometimes miss very strong trends that never pull back.
  • On a new high: buy when the price exceeds its high of the last 20 or 50 sessions. You don't miss any big trend, but you get in at a higher price. It's close to the breakout in lesson 26.

3. Exit with a trailing stop

This is the most important block. A trend follower generally sets no target: they don't know how far the trend will go. They use a trailing stop that rises with the price but never comes back down.

ATR trailing stop = highest price reached since entry − 2 × ATR

The stop can only go up. When the price closes below it, you exit.

The ATR (lesson 16) adapts the stop distance to volatility: the choppier the market, the further away the stop, so you don't get taken out by mere noise. Other traders use the 50-day moving average or the last low as a trailing stop. The principle is the same.

A trade from start to finish (fictional example)

A €10,000 account, 1% risk per trade, i.e. €100. The fictional share Norvel is in an uptrend: 50-day average above the 200-day, rising highs and lows. After a pullback towards its 20-day average, it heads back up. Its ATR is €1.50 (assumed constant for simplicity).

  • Entry at €61.00. Initial stop: 61 − 2 × 1.50 = €58.00. Risk per share: €3.
  • Size: 100 / 3 = 33.3, so 33 shares (€99 of actual risk).

Here's how the trailing stop moves, week by week:

WeekHighest price since entryTrailing stop (high − €3)
1€63.00€60.00
2€66.00€63.00
3€66.00 (pullback to €64.20)€63.00 (unchanged)
4€70.00€67.00
5€73.50€70.50
6€73.50 (the price drops)exit at €70.50

Result: 70.50 − 61.00 = €9.50 per share, i.e. 33 × 9.50 = €313.50, or +3.2R (9.50 / 3). Notice two things. First, Léa (lesson 24) would have banked at 2R around €67; the trailing stop let the trade go further. Second, you never exit at the top (€73.50): the trend follower always gives back part of the gain. That's the price of not getting out too early.

The results profile: lots of small losses, a few big gains

Trend following has a very particular profile: a low win rate (often 30 to 40%) offset by rare but very large gains. Here's a fictional series of 10 trades, in R:

Trade12345678910
Result−1−1+0.4−1−1+6.2−1−0.6+2.8−1

Only 3 winners out of 10 (30%), and yet the total is +2.8R, i.e. €280 with 1R = €100. But look: without trade no. 6, the total falls to −3.4R. The entire performance rests on one or two big winners. Practical consequences:

  • Never cut a winner too early: if you'd banked trade no. 6 at +2R out of fear, the series would be a loser.
  • Take every signal: you don't know in advance which one will be the big winner. Skipping a few "on a hunch" risks missing exactly that one.
  • Be ready for losing streaks: with a 30% win rate, a streak of 8 losses in a row is common (lesson 23). Hence the importance of a small risk per trade.

Weaknesses to know about

  • Trendless markets: in a range, every small move looks like the start of a trend, then reverses. You rack up small losses one after another (this is called getting whipsawed). Some traders filter with the slope of the 200-day average or only act if the price is clearly above it.
  • Sudden reversals: a gap on bad news can jump over the trailing stop (lesson 2).
  • Psychology: watching a +5R gain shrink to +3R before the exit is very frustrating. Many traders crack and go back to fixed targets, which removes the method's edge.

Key takeaways

  • Trend following bets that lasting moves carry on for a while. You follow, you don't predict.
  • Three blocks: identify the trend (highs / lows, moving averages), enter on a pullback or a new high, exit with a trailing stop.
  • ATR trailing stop = highest price since entry − 2 × ATR; it only goes up.
  • Typical profile: 30 to 40% win rate, lots of small losses, a few very big gains that make all the performance.
  • The strategy suffers in ranges and requires accepting that you'll give back part of your gains.
  • Cutting a winner too early or skipping signals destroys the expectancy.

Exercise

  1. A share trades at €44. Its 50-day moving average is at €45, its 200-day at €48. Can you look for a buy here as a trend follower in an uptrend? Why?
  2. An €8,000 account, 1% risk. You enter at €25.00 on a share whose ATR is €0.80, with an initial stop at 2 × ATR. Where's the stop, how many shares do you buy, and how much do you invest?
  3. As the trade from question 2 continues (ATR constant at €0.80), the highs reached each week are €26.50, €28.00, €27.20, then €29.60. Calculate the trailing stop each week. If the price then drops and you exit at that stop, what's your gain in euros and in R?
  4. A trend-following strategy wins 35% of the time, with an average gain of 2.6R and an average loss of 1R. What's its expectancy?
  5. Food for thought: after 7 losses in a row with your trend strategy, a new signal appears. You're hesitating to take it. What would you say to someone in this situation?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. No. The price is below the 50-day average, itself below the 200-day: the setup is rather bearish. A trend follower in an uptrend doesn't buy here. (A trader who accepts short selling, lesson 6, might look for a sell here, depending on their plan.)
  2. Stop: 25.00 − 2 × 0.80 = €23.40, i.e. €1.60 of risk per share. Allowed risk: 1% of €8,000 = €80. Size: 80 / 1.60 = 50 shares. Amount invested: 50 × 25 = €1,250.
  3. Stop = high − €1.60, never moving down: week 1: 26.50 − 1.60 = €24.90; week 2: 28.00 − 1.60 = €26.40; week 3: 27.20 − 1.60 = €25.60, lower than €26.40, so the stop stays at €26.40; week 4: 29.60 − 1.60 = €28.00. Exit at €28.00: a gain of €3.00 per share, i.e. 50 × 3 = €150, or 3 / 1.60 ≈ +1.9R.
  4. Expectancy = 0.35 × 2.6 − 0.65 × 1 = 0.91 − 0.65 = +0.26R per trade. Positive, despite nearly two losses in three.
  5. Seven losses in a row are normal for a strategy with a 30–40% win rate (lesson 23). Signals are independent: the next one is no better or worse because the previous ones lost. In trend following, it's often after a long ranging phase, and therefore a run of losses, that the big trend that pays for everything arrives. If you stick to your 1% risk, those 7 losses cost about 7%: bearable. The right question isn't "do I feel like it?" but "does the signal follow the plan?". If yes, you take it. If the losses exceed what your backtest predicted, you do a cool-headed review, not a gut-feeling choice.

Next lesson: strategy 2, the breakout. Spotting a zone of compression, getting in when the price escapes from it, and protecting yourself against false breakouts.

26.html:
When the spring uncoils

You've surely seen this kind of chart: for weeks, a share marks time between two levels, then suddenly it takes off. The breakout strategy means spotting these zones of compression and getting in the moment the price escapes from them. It's the second strategy in module 5. It's a cousin of trend following (lesson 25): you try to catch the start of a move rather than its middle. Its great enemy has a name: the false breakout.

The logic of a breakout

Remember lesson 10: resistance is a zone where sellers have regularly had the upper hand. As long as the price keeps stalling there, there's a balance between buyers and sellers. When it clearly breaks through, it means the sellers at that level have been "absorbed" and an imbalance has been created.

Several forces then amplify the move:

  • short sellers positioned below the resistance see their buy stops triggered, creating extra buying;
  • traders who were waiting for the breakout get in at the same time;
  • investors who were hesitating make up their minds when they see the price "validate" the level.

The same reasoning applies on the downside: the break of support can trigger a fall.

The ingredients of a good breakout

1. A clear, tested zone

A well-defined range, with resistance touched at least two or three times. The more obvious the zone, the more people are watching it, and the more likely the breakout is to be followed. The triangles and rectangles from lesson 17 are ideal zones.

2. Compressed volatility

Before good breakouts, volatility often falls: candles shrink, the ATR drops, Bollinger Bands tighten (lesson 16). The market is "holding its breath".

3. Rising volume

This is the most important filter. A breakout accompanied by volume well above average (for example 1.5 to 2 times the 20-session average) shows that real buyers are committing. A breakout on low volume is suspicious (lesson 12: volume confirms or contradicts).

4. A favourable context

An upside breakout is more likely to succeed if the underlying trend (weekly, lesson 8) is already up and the overall market (the index) is supportive.

Three ways to enter

MethodHowAdvantageDrawback
Stop ordera buy stop order placed just above resistance (lesson 4)you never miss a breakoutyou get caught by lots of intraday false breakouts
At the closewait for the daily candle to close abovefilters out some false breakoutsyou get in higher
On the retestwait for the price to come back and test the old resistance, now supportbetter price, tighter stopthe retest doesn't always come: you miss moves

A complete example (fictional)

An €8,000 account, 1% risk per trade, i.e. €80. The fictional share Alvéa has been oscillating for six weeks between €48 (support) and €52 (resistance touched three times). The Bollinger Bands are tightening. One day, it closes at €52.40 on twice its average volume.

  • Entry at the close: €52.40.
  • Stop: if the price falls clearly back into the range, the breakout has failed. It goes at €50.80, below the upper middle of the range. Risk: €1.60 per share.
  • Size: 80 / 1.60 = 50 shares, i.e. €2,620 invested.
  • Target: use the projection of the range height.

Breakout target = broken level + height of the range

Here: 52 + (52 − 48) = €56.

Target gain: 56 − 52.40 = €3.60 per share. Ratio: 3.60 / 1.60 = 2.25R. The trade is acceptable under a plan requiring at least 2R (lesson 24).

Retest variant: if you wait for the price to come back to €52.20 before buying, with the same stop, your risk falls to €1.40 and your ratio rises to 3.80 / 1.40 ≈ 2.7R. But if the price heads straight to €56 without coming back, you get nothing.

The big trap: the false breakout

A false breakout is when the price breaks through the level, triggers the buyers' orders... then immediately drops back into the range. It's very common, especially:

  • on overly obvious levels, where lots of stop orders have accumulated: big players can push the price just above to sell into the resulting wave of buying;
  • when volume doesn't follow;
  • just before an important announcement (lessons 30 and 31), which can turn everything upside down.

How do you protect yourself? You can't avoid them all. You accept them as a cost of the job, with three rules:

  1. Always have a stop in place: if the price comes back into the range, you get out, no arguing.
  2. A small risk per trade: the breakout strategy often has a modest win rate, with runs of false breakouts.
  3. Filters: volume, a close above the level, trend context.

A side note: some traders deliberately exploit false breakouts, selling when the price re-enters the range. That's a form of mean reversion, the subject of lesson 27.

Watch out for gaps

If you hold your position overnight, remember lesson 2: a gap can jump over your stop. A failed breakout followed by bad news can make the share open straight below your stop. That's why you generally avoid opening a breakout position on the eve of results.

Key takeaways

  • A breakout means getting in when the price leaves a range or a zone of compression.
  • The best signals: a clear, tested zone, compressed volatility beforehand, sharply rising volume during.
  • Three possible entries: stop order, close, retest. Each has its trade-off between precision and missed opportunities.
  • Classic target: broken level + height of the range.
  • False breakouts are common: mandatory stop, small risk, filters.
  • Avoid breakouts just before a major announcement.

Exercise

  1. A share has been moving between €30 and €33 for two months. It breaks resistance on the upside. What's the target based on the projection of the range height?
  2. A €6,000 account, 1% risk. You enter at €33.20 with a stop at €32.20. How many shares do you buy? What's the risk/reward ratio with the target from question 1?
  3. Two breakouts of the same type: the first happens on volume equal to 0.7 times the average, the second on 2.5 times the average. Which one inspires more confidence, and why?
  4. Take the position from question 2. The breakout fails and, after bad news published in the evening, the share opens the next day at €31.90. Your stop executes at that price. How much do you lose, in euros and in R?
  5. Food for thought: why are breakouts of levels "that everyone can see" often the most treacherous?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Height of the range: 33 − 30 = €3. Target: 33 + 3 = €36.
  2. Allowed risk: 1% of €6,000 = €60. Risk per share: 33.20 − 32.20 = €1.00. Size: 60 shares (€1,992 invested). Target gain: 36 − 33.20 = €2.80. Ratio: 2.80 / 1.00 = 2.8R.
  3. The second (2.5 times the average). Strong volume shows that lots of buyers are genuinely committing above resistance. A breakout on low volume may just be an isolated move, easily pushed back: it's a typical false-breakout candidate.
  4. Loss per share: 33.20 − 31.90 = €1.30. Total: 60 × 1.30 = €78, i.e. −1.3R instead of the planned −1R. The gap cost an extra 0.3R. It's still bearable because the size was calculated for a 1% risk, and that's the whole point of the rule.
  5. Because lots of orders accumulate there: short sellers' buy stops, breakout traders' entry orders. This mass of orders is liquidity (lesson 3) much sought after by big players, who can sell large quantities into the wave of buying triggered just above the level. Once those orders have been "used up", nobody is left to buy, and the price falls back. Hence the value of waiting for confirmation (close, volume, retest) rather than buying at the first cent above.

Next lesson: strategy 3, mean reversion. Buying excessive falls, selling excessive rises, and not getting flattened by a trend.

27.html:
The elastic that snaps back

The two previous strategies (trend following and breakout) bet that the move will continue. Today's bets the opposite: that a price that has gone too far from its "normal" level will come back to it, like an overstretched elastic band. This is mean reversion. It has a very different profile: you win often, but little, and the danger comes from the rare but enormous loss. Understanding this contrast is one of the main goals of module 5.

The starting idea

Over short periods, prices overshoot. A minor piece of bad news, a big seller in a hurry, a bout of panic, and the share drops 8% in three days without anything fundamental having changed. When the excess calms down, the price often returns towards its recent average.

Mean reversion: buying when the price is abnormally low compared with its recent average (or selling when it's abnormally high), and getting out when it returns to it.

The whole problem is telling a temporary excess from a real change. A share falling because the company has just announced massive losses may never "come back" to its old price. This is called catching a falling knife.

The tools for measuring the excess

You already know them:

  • Bollinger Bands (lesson 16): the lower band is 2 standard deviations below the 20-day moving average. A price that touches or breaks through it is statistically "far" from its average.
  • The RSI (lesson 14): below 30 is called oversold; above 70, overbought. Remember the warning from lesson 14: in a strong trend, the RSI can stay in an extreme zone for a long time.
  • Distance from the moving average (lesson 13): for example, a price 5% below its 20-day average.
  • Support and resistance (lesson 10): the bottom of a range is a natural place to buy.

Context decides everything

Mean reversion works well in a trendless, ranging market. It's dangerous in a strong trend: there, the "excesses" aren't anomalies, they're the move itself.

Trend following (lesson 25)Mean reversion
Betthe move continuesthe move reverses
Favourable marketclear trendrange, no trend
Typical win ratelow (30 to 40%)high (55 to 70%)
Size of gainsa few very big gainslots of small gains
The dangerlong streaks of small lossesone big loss that wipes everything out
Psychologyhard to live with day to daypleasant... until the day it breaks

A simple filter: only buy excessive falls if the 200-day moving average is flat or rising, and the price stays within an identified range. If the 200-day is plunging, stay out.

A complete example (fictional)

A €10,000 account, 1% risk per trade, i.e. €100. The fictional share Brévan has been oscillating between €27 and €32 for four months, with a flat 200-day average. After three down sessions, it touches €27.90: below its lower Bollinger Band, RSI at 24. Its 20-day moving average is at €29.00. The next day, a bullish candle forms.

  • Entry: €28.10.
  • Stop: below the bottom of the range and the recent low, at €27.20. Risk: €0.90 per share.
  • Size: 100 / 0.90 = 111.1, so 111 shares, i.e. €3,119.10 invested (€99.90 of actual risk).
  • Target: the return to the 20-day average, €29.00. Target gain: €0.90, i.e. 1R.
  • Time exit: if the price hasn't returned towards the average within 5 sessions, get out. The starting idea (a quick rebound) hasn't materialised.

A ratio of only 1R? Yes, that's typical: you aim for a modest return, but one that happens often. If the strategy wins 65% of the time with an average gain of 0.8R (you sometimes exit a little before the target) and an average loss of 1R, its expectancy is 0.65 × 0.8 − 0.35 × 1 = +0.17R per trade (lesson 22). Decent, but fragile: it depends entirely on respecting the stop.

The disaster scenario: no stop

Imagine that, convinced "it's bound to bounce", you didn't put a stop on Brévan. Bad news comes out, the range breaks to the downside (a breakout, lesson 26!), and the share slides to €22. Your loss: 111 × (28.10 − 22) = €677.10, about 6.8R. With average gains of 0.8R, you need about 8 to 9 winning trades just to wipe out this single loss.

That's the classic mean-reversion trap: the strategy feels easy, with weeks of small gains, and tempts you to "give the losing trade a chance", or even to buy more lower down to bring your average price down. Many retail accounts have been destroyed this way. The rule is absolute: no mean reversion without a stop, and never add to a losing position outside your plan.

Good practice

  • Choose assets that oscillate: major indices and stable large caps lend themselves better to mean reversion than small speculative stocks or crypto.
  • Avoid excesses caused by real news: a 15% drop on results day (lesson 31) isn't an "excess", it's new information.
  • Use a time exit: a rebound that doesn't come is a signal in itself.
  • Diversify over time: lots of small trades, each with limited risk.
  • Combine approaches with care: some traders trend-follow on the weekly and use mean reversion on the daily, in the direction of the trend (buying pullbacks in an uptrend). That's actually Léa's setup in lesson 24.

Key takeaways

  • Mean reversion bets that a price too far from its recent average will return to it.
  • Tools: Bollinger Bands, RSI, distance from the moving average, range boundaries.
  • It works in trendless markets and suffers in strong trends.
  • Profile: high win rate, small gains, and a rare risk of a big loss.
  • A single uncut loss can wipe out weeks of gains: mandatory stop, never averaging down outside the plan.
  • Add a time exit: if the rebound doesn't come quickly, get out.

Exercise

  1. Two shares have an RSI of 25. Share A has been in a range for six months, with a flat 200-day average. Share B is below a sharply falling 200-day average and has just published disappointing results. On which one can a mean-reversion trader look for a buy? Why?
  2. A €5,000 account, 1% risk. You buy at €15.40, stop at €14.90, target at the 20-day average, €16.10. How many shares do you buy? What's the risk/reward ratio?
  3. A mean-reversion strategy wins 68% of the time, with an average gain of 0.7R and an average loss of 1R. Calculate its expectancy. With 1R = €50, how much can you hope to make over 40 trades (before fees)?
  4. With this same strategy, a trader forgets their stop and loses 5R on a single trade. How many average winning trades does it take to wipe out this loss?
  5. Food for thought: trend following bets that the move continues, mean reversion that it reverses. How can both have a positive expectancy?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. On share A. It's in a trendless environment, where excesses tend to correct. Share B combines an underlying downtrend with genuinely bad news: its low RSI reflects a real change, not a temporary excess. It's the "falling knife".
  2. Allowed risk: €50. Risk per share: 15.40 − 14.90 = €0.50. Size: 50 / 0.50 = 100 shares (€1,540 invested). Target gain: 16.10 − 15.40 = €0.70. Ratio: 0.70 / 0.50 = 1.4R.
  3. Expectancy = 0.68 × 0.7 − 0.32 × 1 = 0.476 − 0.32 ≈ +0.156R per trade. With 1R = €50, about €7.80 per trade, i.e. about €312 over 40 trades. A real but thin edge, which fees (lesson 22) can reduce significantly.
  4. 5 / 0.7 ≈ 7.1: you need 8 winning trades to wipe out this single loss. For a strategy that wins about 2 trades in 3, that's a dozen trades' worth of work lost to one forgotten stop.
  5. Because they don't work in the same conditions or over the same horizons. Markets alternate between trending phases (where trend following wins and mean reversion loses) and ranging phases (the reverse). Prices also often show short-term excesses (a few days) within longer-term trends (months). Each strategy captures a different behaviour. Neither wins all the time, which is why you need to know in what context you're using yours.

Next lesson: backtesting. How to test a strategy on the past without telling yourself stories.

28.html:
Why test before you risk

You now have three strategies (lessons 25 to 27) and a plan to frame them (lesson 24). But one question remains open: does it actually work? A strategy's expectancy (lesson 22) can't be guessed; it has to be measured. Backtesting means applying your rules to past data, as if you'd followed them at the time, to see what they would have produced. It's a wonderful tool... and a wonderful machine for fooling yourself. This lesson teaches you to use it honestly.

The principle

Backtest: a simulation of strictly applying trading rules to a price history, to estimate their performance (expectancy, drawdown, number of trades).

Two ways of doing it:

  • Manually: you scroll through a chart candle by candle (many platforms have a "replay" mode), hiding what comes next, and note every trade your plan would have taken. Slow, but very instructive: you learn to recognise your setup.
  • Automatically: you code the rules (in a spreadsheet, in Python, or with a platform's tool) and the computer applies them to years of data. Fast, but it requires perfectly precise rules. We'll come back to this in lesson 39.

In both cases, the basic condition is the same: unambiguous rules. If a rule says "enter when the trend looks solid", the backtest is worthless, because you'll interpret it knowing what happened next.

The numbers to measure

Here's the fictional result of a manual backtest of 20 trades, in R. In order: +2.1; −1; −1; +1.8; −1; +2.5; −1; −1; −1; +2.0; −0.5; +3.2; −1; −1; +1.5; −1; +2.2; −1; −1; +0.8.

MetricDefinitionValue
Number of tradeshow many times the setup appeared20
Win ratewinning trades / total8 / 20 = 40%
Average gainsum of gains / number of winners16.1 / 8 ≈ 2.01R
Average losssum of losses / number of losers11.5 / 12 ≈ 0.96R
Total resultsum of all trades+4.6R
Expectancytotal result / number of trades+0.23R
Profit factorsum of gains / sum of losses16.1 / 11.5 = 1.40
Maximum drawdownworst fall from a peak (lesson 23)3.0R (from +3.4R to +0.4R)

Profit factor = total gains / total losses

Above 1, the strategy makes money; below 1, it loses. Between 1.3 and 2 is already good; above 3, suspect a mistake.

An expectancy of +0.23R is promising. But 20 trades is far too few to draw conclusions: as we saw in lesson 22, chance dominates in small samples. Aim for at least 100 trades, across varied market periods (rising, falling, ranging).

Don't forget fees

Add 0.1R of fees and slippage per trade (commission, spread, worse-than-expected execution, lesson 3). The total drops from +4.6R to +2.6R, the expectancy from +0.23R to +0.13R, and the profit factor from 1.40 to about 1.20. Nearly half the edge has gone. A backtest without fees is a wrong backtest.

Five ways to fool yourself

1. Overfitting

This is trap number one. You test a 20-day moving average: meh. You try the 23, the 27, the 31: the 27 gives superb results. You add an RSI filter, tweak the threshold to 34... After 200 attempts, you're bound to find a combination that would have been brilliant on that particular data, by pure chance. It has "learnt the past by heart", like a student who knows the exam answers without understanding the course. On the future, it collapses.

Warning signs: lots of parameters, very precise settings (27 rather than 20 or 30), results that fall apart if you change a parameter slightly.

2. Look-ahead bias

Unwittingly using information you didn't yet have at the moment of the decision. Example: deciding to buy "at the opening price if the day closes higher". At the open, you don't know the close yet! In a manual backtest, it's also catching a glimpse of what comes next on the chart out of the corner of your eye.

3. Survivorship bias

You test your strategy on the current 40 CAC 40 stocks since 2010. Problem: those companies are in the index today precisely because they did well. The ones that fell and left the index have vanished from your test. Result: inflated performance. You'd need to test on the index's composition at each date.

4. Unrealistic execution

Assuming you always buy at the exact signal price, with no spread, no gap, on illiquid shares where your order would have moved the price. Reality is always a bit worse than the backtest.

5. A sample that's too short or too uniform

A buying strategy tested only between 2020 and 2021, a period of strong rises, will look excellent. It needs to have been through crashes, ranges and rate rises.

The honest method: in-sample / out-of-sample

To fight overfitting, you split the data in two:

  1. Training period (in-sample), for example 2012 to 2019: you develop your rules on it.
  2. Validation period (out-of-sample), for example 2020 to 2025: you don't touch it until your rules are frozen. Then you test, only once.

If the expectancy goes from +0.40R in training to +0.05R in validation, the strategy was mainly fitted to noise. If it stays in the same ballpark (for example +0.25R then +0.18R), that's encouraging. Moderate deterioration is normal; a collapse is a signal to stop.

And even a good backtest guarantees nothing: markets change. It eliminates bad ideas more than it proves good ones. The next step, before real money, is paper trading (lesson 29).

Key takeaways

  • A backtest applies precise rules to the past to measure expectancy, win rate, profit factor and drawdown.
  • Profit factor = total gains / total losses; above 1, the strategy makes money.
  • You need at least 100 trades across varied markets, and always include fees and slippage.
  • Traps: overfitting, look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, unrealistic execution, an overly favourable period.
  • Split the data into training and validation, and test on validation only once.
  • A backtest that looks too good is more often a mistake than a treasure.

Exercise

  1. A backtest gives these 10 trades, in R: +2; −1; −1; +3; −1; −1; −1; +1.5; −1; +2. Calculate the win rate, the total result, the expectancy and the profit factor.
  2. For the same series, calculate the cumulative result after each trade and find the maximum drawdown in R.
  3. Add 0.15R of fees per trade to this series. What happens to the total result and the expectancy?
  4. A friend has tested 500 combinations of parameters on the DAX between 2015 and 2024. The best shows an expectancy of +0.8R and a profit factor of 3.5. He wants to use it with real money from Monday. What do you advise?
  5. Food for thought: you test a strategy on the current 40 CAC 40 stocks since 2005. Why are your results likely to be too optimistic, and how could you do better?
Answers (have a go first!)
  1. Winners: 4 out of 10, i.e. 40%. Gains: 2 + 3 + 1.5 + 2 = 8.5R. Losses: 6 × 1 = 6R. Total result: +2.5R. Expectancy: 2.5 / 10 = +0.25R. Profit factor: 8.5 / 6 ≈ 1.42.
  2. Cumulative: 2; 1; 0; 3; 2; 1; 0; 1.5; 0.5; 2.5. The peak is 3 (after the 4th trade), the next trough is 0 (after the 7th). Maximum drawdown: 3R, i.e. 3% of the account with a 1% risk per trade.
  3. Total fees are 10 × 0.15 = 1.5R. Total result: 2.5 − 1.5 = +1.0R. Expectancy: +0.10R per trade, versus +0.25R before fees. More than half the edge disappears.
  4. After 500 attempts, finding an exceptional combination is almost guaranteed by chance: it's a textbook case of overfitting, and a profit factor of 3.5 is suspicious. Advice: check that the results hold up with neighbouring parameters, test on a validation period never used before (for example 2025 and 2026), add realistic fees and slippage, then go through a paper trading phase (lesson 29) before risking small sums.
  5. It's survivorship bias: the stocks in the index today are the ones that succeeded. Those that fell sharply, were taken over or went bust and have left the index since 2005 aren't in your test, even though your strategy might have traded them (and lost on them). To do better: use the index's historical composition at each date, or a database that includes companies that have disappeared.

Next lesson: paper trading and the trading journal. Practising without real money, then recording every trade so you can improve.

29.html:
From the lab to the real world

Your plan is written (lesson 24), your strategy has passed the backtest (lesson 28). Does that mean you should put your money on it tomorrow? Not yet. A backtest tells you what your rules would have done. It doesn't tell you what you will do in real time, when you have to decide without knowing what comes next, with prices moving and emotions rising. This lesson presents two tools that bridge the gap: paper trading to practise, and the trading journal to improve, now and throughout your life as a trader.

Paper trading: practising without money

Paper trading: applying your plan in real time, on the current market, but with fictional money, on a demo account or in a simple spreadsheet.

Most brokers offer a free demo account, with real prices. You can also write down your orders by hand before the market moves.

What paper trading teaches you

  • Spotting your setup live, without knowing what comes next on the chart (no way to cheat as in a backtest).
  • Mastering your platform: placing a limit order, a stop, modifying an order (lesson 4). A typing error on a demo costs nothing; for real, it can cost a lot.
  • Testing your routine: do you really have time to do your analysis every evening? Is your plan compatible with your classes and exams?
  • Checking that the strategy behaves as expected: number of signals, win rate, rough expectancy.

What it doesn't teach you

  • Fear and greed. Cutting a loss of €100 of fictional money is easy. Cutting a loss of €100 of real money, a week's food shopping, is much harder.
  • Real execution: on a demo, your orders are often filled perfectly, with no slippage, even on large sizes.
  • The weight of time: on a demo, people tend to take more trades and risks they'd never take for real.

Rules for useful paper trading

  1. Same capital as your future real account. A €100,000 demo when you have €3,000 skews everything.
  2. Same plan, same risk rules, no exceptions.
  3. Count fees as if they were real.
  4. No resetting after a bad run.
  5. A set duration: for example 30 to 50 trades, or two to three months of swing trading.

Moving to real money, step by step

After paper trading, you don't jump straight to your normal risk. A sensible progression: a few dozen real trades with a much reduced risk (0.25% to 0.5% of the account), then the risk set out in your plan (1% at most) if you've stuck to your rules. The aim of this phase isn't to make money: it's to check that you can apply your plan when it's your own money at stake.

The trading journal: your most powerful tool

Most traders who lose don't know why they lose. Is their strategy bad? Or are they not following it? Without data, there's no way to answer. The journal is the logbook where you record every trade, winning or losing, real or fictional.

What to record

Before the tradeAfter the trade
date, asset, direction (buy / sell)exit price and date
setup used (trend, breakout, mean reversion)result in euros and in R
entry price, stop, targetreason for exit (stop, target, time, manual decision)
position size and risk in eurosplan followed: yes / no (and if not, which rule)
screenshot of the chart at entryemotional state, what you'd do differently

A spreadsheet is more than enough. The key is to fill it in every time, especially after the trades you're not proud of.

A journal that talks (fictional example)

Here are eight of Nathan's trades, swing trading French shares, with 1R = €100 (the trades are made up for the example).

No.ShareSetupResultPlan followed?Comment
1Orangetrend+1.8Ryescalm
2Stellantisbreakout−1Ryesfalse breakout
3Danonemean reversion+0.9Ryes
4Keringbreakout−2.3Rnostop moved "to give it some room"
5Saint-Gobaintrend+2.6Ryes
6Capgeminibreakout−1Ryes
7Renaultnone−1.5Rnobought on impulse after a news item
8Michelintrend−1Ryes

Raw result: −1.5R, i.e. −€150. Nathan could conclude that his strategy doesn't work. But the journal tells a different story:

  • the 6 trades that followed the plan add up to +1.8 − 1 + 0.9 + 2.6 − 1 − 1 = +2.3R, about +0.38R per trade;
  • the 2 trades outside the plan add up to −3.8R.

The problem isn't the strategy, it's discipline. Without a journal, Nathan might have changed method; with one, he knows exactly what to fix: stop moving his stops, stop trading on impulse.
